me: YOCO proposes in-situ multiply arithmetic (IMA) using charge-domain computation and time-domain accumulation, combined with hybrid ReRAM-SRAM memory to balance efficiency and density. An IMC-friendly attention pipeline accelerates transformer inference.
nv: 8-bit in-situ multiply arithmetic achieving 123.8 TOPS/W via efficient charge-domain compute and time-domain accumulation.

mx.speedup: 3.9-19.9x energy, 6.8-33.6x throughput

th: Hybrid analog in-memory compute for efficient transformer inference

t: High Energy-efficiency and Low latency In-Memory Computing using Analog Accumulator and In-Memory ADC with shared References
pb: In-memory computing array ADCs require high area overhead for data conversion; traditional approaches sacrifice linearity and energy efficiency.
me: A 256x128 in-memory array uses dual-8T SRAM bitcells for ternary weight storage and read-write decoupling. Bit-slicing with charge-sharing binary weighted accumulator (CHA) handles multi-bit input. Read WWL Under Drive enables low-current variation.
nv: Reconfigurable in-memory ADC with shared references achieving 9x area overhead reduction and 1146 TOPS/W through efficient accumulation.
th: Shared-reference in-memory ADC for efficient analog compute arrays

t: PIMDup: An Optimized Deduplication Design on a Real Processing-in-Memory System
pb: Data deduplication requires scanning entire datasets during chunking, causing excessive data movement between memory and compute. Conventional architectures (GPUs, FPGAs) suffer from von Neumann bottlenecks; processing-in-memory (PIM) systems face unique constraints including restricted inter-DPU sharing and high DPU-CPU communication overhead.
me: PIMDup optimizes deduplication on UPMEM DPUs through efficient parallelization, DPU-friendly chunking techniques that avoid multiplication, and reduced data transfer volumes between DPU and CPU, maintaining 100% result consistency.
nv: First deduplication system co-designed for PIM constraints: elimination of inter-DPU sharing limits through parallelization and DPU-friendly chunking without native multiplication.

mx.speedup: 1.67x over CPU

th: PIM-optimized deduplication with reduced data movement

t: DataMaestro: A Versatile and Efficient Data Streaming Engine Bringing Decoupled Memory Access To Dataflow Accelerators
pb: DNN inference on dataflow accelerators faces performance bottlenecks from data movement; accelerators lack decoupled access/execute architectures to mitigate memory access inefficiency and bank conflicts.
me: DataMaestro is a programmable data streaming unit supporting flexible access patterns, fine-grained prefetch and bank-conflict mitigation through dynamic addressing mode switching, and on-the-fly data manipulation to reduce memory footprints. Integrated with Tensor Core-like GeMM and quantization accelerators on RISC-V host with FPGA prototype and VLSI synthesis validation.
nv: Decoupled access/execute architecture for dataflow accelerators with programmable prefetch, dynamic bank-conflict resolution, and configurable on-the-fly data manipulation.

mx.speedup: 1.05-21.39x over SOTA

th: Decoupled access/execute for DNN dataflow accelerators with programmable streaming

t: TAXI: Traveling Salesman Problem Accelerator with X-bar-based Ising Macros Powered by SOT-MRAMs and Hierarchical Clustering
pb: Ising solvers with hierarchical clustering for large-scale Traveling Salesman Problems (TSPs) face quality degradation as problem size scales beyond certain extent. Hardware-agnostic approaches underutilize available hardware resources.
me: TAXI uses crossbar (X-bar) based Ising macros solving TSP subproblems via hierarchical clustering without inter-macro data movement, enabling massive parallelism. Spin-Orbit-Torque (SOT) MRAM devices serve as compact, energy-efficient random number generators enabling rapid natural annealing within each macro.
nv: Hardware-algorithm co-design combining Ising solver macros with SOT-MRAM-based random annealing and hierarchical clustering to achieve massive parallelism without inter-macro data movement.

mx.speedup: 8x over SOTA clustering-based Ising solver

th: In-memory crossbar Ising solver with SOT-MRAM annealing for large-scale TSP

t: SplitSync: Bank Group-Level Split-Synchronization for High-Performance DRAM PIM
pb: DRAM PIM architectures with bank-level SIMD parallelism suffer from synchronous execution requiring all banks to activate before computation. Row activation overhead exceeds computation time, limiting performance. Asynchronous approaches reduce overhead but require large shared accumulators per bank, increasing area.
me: Bank group (BG) level split-synchronization: each BG operates asynchronously to hide row activation overhead while operating synchronously within a BG to eliminate shared accumulators. Hybrid approach balances activation hide and area efficiency.
nv: Bank group-level split synchronization strategy enabling asynchronous inter-BG operation with intra-BG synchronization to maintain area efficiency while hiding activation overhead.

mx.speedup: 1.70x vs conventional PIM, 1.06x vs asynchronous PIM
mx.area: 1.5% overhead per processing unit vs conventional PIM

th: Split-synchronization at bank group level for high-performance DRAM PIM

t: STREAMINGGS: Voxel-Based Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting with Memory Optimization and Architectural Support
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) struggles to achieve real-time 90 FPS rendering on mobile devices (currently only 2-9 FPS), with existing accelerators optimizing compute efficiency but ignoring memory efficiency, resulting in redundant DRAM traffic.
me: STREAMINGGS implements fully streaming algorithm-architecture co-design with fine-grained pipelining and transforms from tile-centric rendering (tile-first, load all Gaussians) to memory-centric rendering (stream Gaussian groups, load only touched tiles). This approach reduces DRAM traffic and enables better prefetching and memory utilization on mobile GPUs.
nv: Shift from tile-centric to memory-centric rendering paradigm with streaming architecture enables fine-grained pipelining and dramatically reduces DRAM bandwidth requirements for mobile 3DGS inference.

mx.speedup: 45.7x vs mobile Ampere GPU
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 62.9x energy savings vs mobile Ampere GPU

th: Memory-centric streaming 3DGS accelerator for mobile rendering

t: LearnGraph: A Learning-Based Architecture for Dynamic Graph Processing
pb: Dynamic graph processing systems using conventional array-based architectures suffer from inefficient memory access patterns and poor index management, limiting throughput.
me: Proposes an adaptive tree-based memory manager with two components: (1) hierarchical learned index optimized for graph topology to predict vertex and edge locations, and (2) adaptive tree structure that dynamically reorganizes memory regions based on access patterns.
nv: Integration of learned indexes with topology-aware adaptive memory reorganization for dynamic graph systems.

mx.speedup: 3.4x higher throughput; 1.7x-11x reduction in processing time
mx.other: adaptive memory reorganization overhead

th: Learned-index–driven adaptive memory architecture for graphs

t: 3D-TokSIM: Stacking 3D Memory with Token-Stationary Compute-in-Memory for Speculative LLM Inference
pb: LLM autoregressive decoding faces severe memory bandwidth bottleneck from the logic die; 2D memory solutions cannot overcome this due to limited memory-to-logic bandwidth.
me: Proposes 3D-TokSIM combining 3D memory stacking on logic die with token-stationary compute-in-memory (CIM); uses novel token-stationary dataflow to minimize data movement on logic die, reducing power and balancing compute/memory throughput; architecture exploration allocates CIM resources for higher decoding parallelism.
nv: Token-stationary CIM dataflow for speculative LLM decoding with 3D memory stacking.

mx.speedup: 15.1x throughput vs RTX 3090

th: Token-stationary CIM with 3D memory for LLM speculative decoding

t: A Data-Centric Hardware Accelerator for Efficient Adaptive Radix Tree
pb: Adaptive Radix Tree (ART) operations suffer from redundant tree traversals and high synchronization costs during concurrent read/write operations in databases and key-value stores.
me: Proposes DCART, a data-centric hardware accelerator that exploits temporal and spatial similarities in workloads; coalesces operations targeting the same ART nodes and adaptively caches frequently traversed nodes and their search results.
nv: Data-centric processing model for ART acceleration that coalesces operations and adapts caching based on runtime access patterns.

mx.speedup: 21.1x-44.2x speedup

th: Data-centric ART acceleration via operation coalescing and adaptive caching

t: A Memory-Efficient LLM Accelerator with Q-K Correlation Prediction using Cluster-Based Associative Array for Selective KV Accessing
pb: Autoregressive LLM inference incurs redundant attention computations and high KV cache memory access; full cache retention wastes bandwidth as many key-value pairs contribute minimally to output.
me: Sella hardware-software co-design uses cluster-based associative arrays to predict Q-K correlation scores; a specialized prediction engine identifies low-value KV pairs, enabling selective cache access. ASIC accelerator exploits sparsity in attention patterns.
nv: Q-K correlation prediction via associative arrays to dynamically filter KV cache access without model retraining.

mx.other: 66% off-chip memory reduction, <1% accuracy loss

th: KV cache selective access

t: A Full-system, Programmable, and Extensible In-Memory Computing Simulation Framework for Deep Learning
pb: Designing scalable, programmable IMC platforms for modern generative AI (LLMs, DiTs) lacks simulation infrastructure that accurately models device-level physics while supporting full-stack software integration.
me: IMCsim provides full-system simulation: (1) ISA extensions for tensor operations, (2) mappable to eNVM-, SRAM-, or digital IMC architectures, (3) validated against silicon prototypes (22nm MRAM, 28nm SRAM), (4) enables PPA trade-off exploration across workloads.
nv: First full-stack IMC simulator bridging device physics and AI workload execution with validated silicon correlation.

mx.other: simulation accuracy vs silicon, PPA trade-offs

th: IMC full-system simulator

t: Ariadne: A Hotness-Aware and Size-Adaptive Compressed Swap Technique for Fast Application Relaunch and Reduced CPU Usage on Mobile Devices
pb: Mobile devices under memory pressure use ZRAM (RAM-based compressed swap) to defer app eviction, but ZRAM prolongs relaunch latency and wastes CPU time because it applies uniform compression settings regardless of data hotness, does not differentiate compression chunk size, and lacks prefetching of soon-to-be-needed decompressed data.
me: Ariadne introduces three coordinated techniques: (1) a low-overhead hotness-aware data organization scheme that classifies anonymous memory pages as hot, warm, or cold based on observed relaunch access patterns, allowing reuse of hotness labels across consecutive relaunches; (2) a size-adaptive compression scheme that uses small chunk sizes for hot/warm data (enabling fast decompression on the critical relaunch path) and large chunk sizes for cold data (improving compression ratio); and (3) a proactive decompression scheme that predicts the next set of pages needed during relaunch and decompresses them in advance to overlap decompression with computation.
nv: Hotness-aware adaptive compression chunk sizing that applies small fast-decompressing chunks to relaunch-critical data and large high-ratio chunks to cold data, combined with proactive decompression based on observed relaunch locality.

mx.speedup: 50% reduction in application relaunch latency vs ZRAM
mx.other: 15% reduction in CPU usage for compression/decompression vs ZRAM

th: hotness-aware adaptive compressed swap for mobile application relaunch optimization

t: Efficient Caching with A Tag-enhanced DRAM
pb: DRAM-based caches (e.g., HBM3-as-cache) suffer from high miss penalties due to two-step tag-then-data access, wasted data movement on cache misses where data is fetched then discarded, and interference between demand requests and miss-fetched data on the data bus. Existing DRAM cache designs cannot perform in-DRAM tag comparison or conditional data response, so they always transfer data regardless of hit/miss status.
me: TDRAM adds small, low-latency metadata/tag mats to an HBM3 die alongside the existing data mats, enabling lockstep tag-and-data access, in-DRAM tag comparison, and conditional data response (data is only transferred to the CPU if the comparison indicates a hit), eliminating wasted data bus transfers on misses. Opportunistic early tag probing allows tag lookups to start before the full row is available, reducing both hit and miss latencies. A flush buffer stores conflicting dirty data on write misses within the DRAM, eliminating data bus turnaround delays caused by writing back dirty evictees before fetching new data.
nv: Adding low-latency tag mats directly to the HBM3 die enabling in-DRAM tag comparison and conditional data response, mirroring SRAM cache semantics (no wasted data transfer on miss) in a DRAM-based cache.

mx.speedup: 1.23x speedup vs state-of-the-art commercial and research DRAM caches
mx.other: 2.65x faster tag checks

th: in-DRAM tag comparison for efficient DRAM-based cache with conditional data response

t: SoMa: Identifying, Exploring, and Understanding the DRAM Communication Scheduling Space for DNN Accelerators
pb: As on-chip buffers on DNN accelerators grow large enough to hold most single-layer weights, single-layer dataflow optimization no longer meaningfully reduces DRAM bandwidth pressure. Multi-layer fusion and DRAM communication scheduling (timing of prefetches and stores across fused layers) remain an open, poorly-characterized optimization problem.
me: SoMa introduces a Tensor-centric Notation (TCN) to formally represent and enumerate DRAM communication scheduling schemes across fused layer groups. An end-to-end scheduling compiler framework explores this space jointly optimizing prefetch timing, data store scheduling, and layer fusion decisions for diverse accelerators and workloads. SoMa has been deployed as a compiler for a commercial accelerator product.
nv: Tensor-centric Notation that formally defines and spans the DRAM communication scheduling space for multi-layer fused DNN execution, enabling systematic compiler-driven exploration beyond single-layer dataflow.

mx.speedup: 2.11x average performance improvement vs. Cocco

th: Compiler-driven DRAM communication scheduling across fused DNN layers

t: AsyncDIMM: Achieving Asynchronous Execution in DIMM-Based Near-Memory Processing
pb: DIMM-based near-memory processing (NMP) architectures cannot efficiently support asynchronous execution between host CPUs and near-memory accelerators (NMAs) because independent memory controllers on both sides cause memory bus contention and potential DRAM errors when issuing concurrent accesses. Existing designs resort to synchronous execution, wasting either host or NMA compute.
me: AsyncDIMM introduces three operational modes on existing memory buses: single access (host or NMA only), concurrent access, and seamless mode switching. An offload-schedule-return mechanism with explicit and implicit synchronization ensures correct memory access semantics across modes. Optimized timing constraints reduce offload latency; a locality-aware switch-recovery method minimizes mode-switch overhead; adaptive batching with timing-division multiplexing notifications improves return bandwidth. Hardware modifications are limited to conventional host and NMA memory controllers and validated on FPGA.
nv: Offload-schedule-return mechanism with dual synchronization modes (explicit and implicit) enabling correct concurrent host+NMA DRAM access on existing unmodified memory buses without protocol changes.

mx.speedup: 1.19x-1.92x over four NMP baselines
mx.other: Up to 2.25x bandwidth utilization uplift; 47% access latency reduction

th: Asynchronous host-NMA co-execution in DIMM-based near-memory processing

t: Gaze into the Pattern: Characterizing Spatial Patterns with Internal Temporal Correlations for Hardware Prefetching
pb: Existing spatial-region hardware prefetchers predict memory access footprints using system-level context features (trigger PC, data address) that fail to capture the intrinsic characteristics of spatial access patterns, resulting in poor flexibility and suboptimal prefetch accuracy across diverse workloads.
me: Gaze extracts footprint-internal temporal correlations — the ordering and timing relationships among cache line accesses within a spatial region — as the primary feature for characterizing and predicting spatial access patterns. This avoids dependence on trigger PC or address-based context lookup. For spatial streaming patterns (very high access density within a region), Gaze applies a dedicated two-stage prefetch approach to suppress over-prefetching: a first stage filters high-density streaming footprints and a second stage applies targeted prefetch decisions to avoid redundant prefetches.
nv: Using footprint-internal temporal correlation (access ordering within spatial regions) rather than external context (trigger PC/address) as the core feature for spatial pattern characterization in a hardware prefetcher.

mx.speedup: 5.7% and 5.4% single-core; 11.4% and 8.8% eight-core IPC improvement vs. PMP and vBerti respectively

th: Spatial hardware prefetching using intra-footprint temporal correlations

t: Rethinking Dead Block Prediction for Intermittent Computing
pb: Existing dead block predictors, designed for conventional always-on systems, are ineffective in energy-harvesting intermittent computing systems because they do not account for power failures that invalidate cache blocks before they can be reused, causing unnecessary leakage energy waste on blocks that are nominally 'live' but will be lost.
me: EDBP (Enhanced Dead Block Predictor) augments existing dead block predictors with a power-failure-aware prediction layer. It identifies cache blocks that, though predicted live by a conventional predictor, are unlikely to be accessed before the next anticipated power failure. These blocks are deactivated (gated off) to eliminate leakage energy, freeing energy budget for forward execution. EDBP is combined with the Cache Decay predictor to achieve near-theoretical-minimum cache leakage across 20 Mediabench and MiBench applications.
nv: Incorporating power failure prediction into dead block identification, enabling leakage reduction for blocks that are live under a conventional model but unreachable due to imminent energy exhaustion.

mx.other: 11.9% performance improvement; 6.5% energy reduction standalone; 20 Mediabench/MiBench applications

th: Power-failure-aware cache dead block prediction for intermittent energy-harvesting systems

t: NOVA: A Novel Vertex Management Architecture for Scalable Graph Processing
pb: Existing graph processing hardware accelerators require temporal graph partitioning to fit the working set into on-chip memory, limiting scalability to large graphs and causing bandwidth inefficiency from repeated DRAM accesses across partition sweeps.
me: NOVA decouples reduction and propagation operations in the vertex-centric graph processing paradigm, allowing the entire working set to reside in off-chip DRAM rather than being partitioned across on-chip memory. On-chip memory is repurposed as a prefetch/access buffer to hide DRAM latency rather than as a traditional cache holding graph state. The design enables spatial tiling across multiple NOVA nodes for scale-out, achieving near-perfect weak and strong scaling. A cycle-accurate gem5-based model validates the architecture.
nv: Decoupling reduction and propagation in the vertex-centric paradigm to eliminate the requirement for temporal graph partitioning, enabling direct DRAM-resident large-graph processing with latency-hiding on-chip buffers.

mx.speedup: 2.35x over PolyGraph on 134M-vertex 2.14B-edge synthetic graph

th: Decoupled reduction-propagation vertex management for scalable large-graph hardware processing

t: PROCA: Programmable Probabilistic Processing Unit Architecture with Accept/Reject Prediction & Multicore Pipelining for Causal Inference
pb: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms for probabilistic programming and causal inference are extremely compute-intensive and inherently sequential, preventing effective parallelization on CPUs and GPUs; existing MCMC accelerators are not programmable across arbitrary posterior distribution forms.
me: PROCA is a programmable MCMC processing unit using processing-in-memory (PIM) function units to generate Markov chain samples. A novel accept/reject prediction methodology predicts whether a proposed sample will be accepted before completing full posterior evaluation, enabling multi-core pipelining: compute for the next sample begins before the current accept/reject decision finalizes. The architecture is programmable to support arbitrary posterior distribution forms compatible with software probabilistic programming frameworks (e.g., PyMC). Implemented using commercial process development kits and validated on 9 benchmarks spanning PyMC tutorials, single-variable problems, and real-world causal inference tasks.
nv: Accept/reject prediction that breaks the sequential dependency of MCMC sampling chains, enabling multi-core pipelined execution of arbitrary posterior distributions with PIM-based sample generation.

mx.speedup: 172-4871x over Intel Xeon Gold CPU; 42-1058x over NVIDIA A100 GPU; 1.765x over SOTA MCMC accelerator
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 9.47x energy efficiency over SOTA MCMC accelerators

th: Programmable PIM-based MCMC accelerator with accept/reject prediction for causal inference

t: ER-DCIM: Error-Resilient Digital CIM Architecture with Run-Time MAC-Cell Error Correction
pb: Digital compute-in-memory (DCIM) macros are susceptible to SRAM cell errors under low-voltage operation (needed for high energy efficiency), but traditional SRAM error correcting codes (ECC) that correct errors in a single read-out row are incompatible with DCIM's simultaneous multi-row readout for MAC computation, leaving MAC-cell errors uncorrected.
me: ER-DCIM introduces three mechanisms: (1) a residue code-based MAC error correction scheme that detects and corrects additive errors in the MAC accumulation result in real time during DCIM computation — the first such mechanism for DCIM; (2) a progressive cell error correction mechanism that identifies and corrects underlying SRAM cell errors incrementally without stalling computation; (3) a mode switcher that repurposes redundant error-resilient logic (reserved for low-voltage protection) to boost performance in high-voltage mode, avoiding area waste.
nv: Residue code-based real-time MAC error correction for digital CIM, the first mechanism to correct additive errors in DCIM MAC results during live computation rather than at the SRAM cell or row level.

mx.other: Maintains accuracy without loss in both low-voltage and high-voltage modes; no accuracy degradation stated vs. baseline

th: Run-time MAC-level error correction for reliable low-voltage digital compute-in-memory

t: GSArch: Breaking Memory Barriers in 3D Gaussian Splatting Training via Architectural Support
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training is bottlenecked by three memory system inefficiencies: redundant off-chip DRAM loads for large 'hot' Gaussians accessed repeatedly across pixels, expensive atomic write operations during gradient accumulation, and severe bank conflicts during on-chip buffer reads during backward propagation.
me: GSArch introduces three architectural mechanisms targeting the three bottlenecks: (1) Hybrid memory management that classifies Gaussians as 'hot' (large, high pixel overlap, repeatedly loaded) or 'cold' and caches hot Gaussians in a fast on-chip buffer to eliminate redundant DRAM fetches; (2) Gradient informativeness filtering that identifies low-contribution gradients and skips their atomic write operations during backward propagation; (3) A rearrangement unit that packs conflicting on-chip memory read requests into non-conflicting bundles to eliminate bank conflicts. These techniques combine to accelerate the backward pass of 3DGS training.
nv: Gaussian 'hotness' classification for hybrid on-chip/off-chip memory management that eliminates the dominant redundant DRAM load pattern in 3DGS training backward propagation.

mx.speedup: Up to 6.49x over A100 GPU; up to 15.42x over Jetson AGX Xavier
mx.energy_or_tops_w: Substantially lower energy consumption (not quantified in abstract)

th: Architectural support for memory-efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting training via hot/cold Gaussian buffering

t: Zebra: Efficient Redundant Array of Zoned Namespace SSDs Enabled by Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA)
pb: Integrating ZNS SSDs into RAID configurations requires handling partial parity updates (PPUs) that arise from ZNS's append-only write semantics; existing metadata-zone-based solutions become performance bottlenecks under high PPU workloads.
me: Zebra exploits the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA), the SSD's internal write buffer in front of each zone, to handle PPUs in-place. By ensuring that parity chunks fit within the ZRWA window, Zebra performs partial parity overrides within the buffer rather than writing to separate metadata zones. A set of complementary techniques maintain high performance and reliability across both large-zone and small-zone ZNS SSD models.
nv: Using the ZRWA (the SSD's native write buffer window) as the target storage for parity partial updates in ZNS RAID, matching the repeated sequential overwrite I/O pattern of PPUs to the ZRWA's random-write capability.

mx.speedup: 1.1x to 4.2x throughput improvement vs RAIZN ZNS RAID system

th: ZNS RAID partial parity management via ZRWA exploitation

t: Multi-Dimensional Vector ISA Extension for Mobile In-Cache Computing
pb: Existing long-vector ISA extensions (RISC-V RVV, Arm SVE) provide only 1D strided and random memory accesses, which cannot efficiently utilize the 8192-lane SIMD width of in-SRAM vector engines built from mobile L2 caches because mobile data-parallel kernels expose limited 1D parallelism (average 635 elements) across multiple multi-dimensional data structures.
me: MVE (Multi-dimensional Vector ISA Extension) introduces up to 4D strided and random vector memory accesses, where each dimension can use stride modes: replicate (stride=0), sequential (stride=1), row-stride (stride=previous_dim x length), or arbitrary CR-configured stride. A dimension-level masked execution mechanism masks entire outer-dimension iterations using a compact mask control register, avoiding expensive per-lane scalar mask computation. The ISA operates on physical registers spanning all in-SRAM compute arrays (8192 lanes of 32-bit data), with a cache-geometry-hiding register abstraction. The MVE controller in the L2 cache flattens multi-dimensional logical register accesses to physical SRAM bitline coordinates, uses a Transpose Memory Unit (TMU) with 8T transpose bit-cells and a crossbar to route data into vertical bit-serial layout, and manages cache coherency by checking L1 presence bits and evicting L1 lines before in-cache writes. Compiler support includes liveness analysis for register width, list-hybrid instruction scheduling, and greedy register allocation to minimize in-cache register spills.
nv: A multi-dimensional vector ISA (up to 4D strided + random memory accesses with dimension-level masked execution) that hides cache geometry from programmers while raising in-cache SIMD lane utilization from 23% to 60% for mobile workloads.

mx.speedup: 2.9x vs Arm Neon; 9.3x vs Adreno 640 GPU; 2.0x vs RISC-V RVV on same in-cache engine; 1.5x vs Duality Cache (SIMT model)
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 8.8x energy reduction vs Arm Neon; 5.2x energy reduction vs Adreno 640 GPU

th: multi-dimensional vector ISA for mobile in-SRAM computing

t: PAISE: PIM-Accelerated Inference Scheduling Engine for Transformer-based LLM
pb: LLM inference on GPUs is memory-bound due to the attention layer's low arithmetic intensity and high memory traffic from frequent KV-cache updates, leading to elevated latency under autoregressive token generation. GPU-only execution under-utilizes available bandwidth for attention operations.
me: PAISE offloads memory-intensive attention operations from an AMD MI100 GPU to HBM-PIM devices via a GPU-PIM heterogeneous scheduling framework. A scheduling algorithm determines per-operation offload decisions based on model configuration (layer type, head count) and PIM hardware specifications (bandwidth, FLOPS). An enhanced PIM kernel implements transaction-wise interleave-batched GEMM, restructuring data layout so multiple attention heads' KV reads are interleaved across PIM banks, maximizing memory-level parallelism within the HBM-PIM device.
nv: Transaction-wise interleave-batched GEMM on HBM-PIM that reorders KV-cache data layout to exploit bank-level parallelism, combined with a model-aware scheduling algorithm that decides which transformer layers to offload.

mx.speedup: up to 48.3% execution time reduction vs GPU-only for attention layer

th: PIM-accelerated LLM attention offloading

t: Marching Page Walks: Batching and Concurrent Page Table Walks for Enhancing GPU Throughput
pb: GPU page table walkers handle only a single walk request at a time, creating severe queuing latency when thousands of concurrent threads simultaneously demand address translation across wide virtual address ranges.
me: Marching Page Walks (MPW) scans the pool of pending walk requests to identify groups that can share memory accesses (e.g., walks to nearby pages sharing a page table entry lookup). It batches these requests and concurrently issues multiple memory instructions per walker to service several walks simultaneously, exploiting the observation that GPU workloads access pages in wide but often co-located address ranges.
nv: Enabling a single GPU page table walker to issue multiple memory instructions concurrently by batching pending walk requests that share page table structure accesses, directly attacking queuing latency rather than walker count.

mx.speedup: 55.6% average GPU performance improvement over baseline
mx.other: 86.7% reduction in page walk queuing latency

th: batched concurrent GPU page table walking to reduce queuing latency

t: Integrating Prefetcher Selection with Dynamic Request Allocation Improves Prefetching Efficiency
pb: Hybrid hardware prefetchers sharing the same MSHRs and bandwidth resources create conflicts where competing prefetch requests from different algorithms negate each other's coverage, and existing prefetcher selection algorithms use inaccurate demand request allocation and coarse-grained selection criteria.
me: Alecto is a prefetcher selection algorithm that intercepts each demand request before routing it to prefetchers. For each demand request, Alecto determines the most suitable prefetcher(s) by evaluating fine-grained per-request suitability metrics (accuracy, coverage, timeliness). It then dynamically routes each demand request only to the prefetcher(s) best suited for that specific access, rather than broadcasting to all prefetchers. This per-request allocation prevents table pollution in temporal prefetchers and reduces resource contention.
nv: Per-demand-request prefetcher selection that routes each request only to the most suitable prefetcher, simultaneously improving accuracy, coverage, and timeliness while drastically reducing prefetcher table energy by avoiding unnecessary training.

mx.speedup: 2.76% IPC improvement (single-core) and 7.56% (eight-core) over Bandit; 5.25% on memory-intensive
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 48% prefetcher table energy reduction; 7% full memory hierarchy energy reduction

th: fine-grained per-request prefetcher selection to reduce hybrid prefetcher conflicts

t: Variable Read Disturbance: An Experimental Analysis of Temporal Variation in DRAM Read Disturbance
pb: DRAM read disturbance (RowHammer/RowPress) mitigation techniques rely on accurate per-row read disturbance threshold (RDT) characterization, but the RDT of individual DRAM rows is not static: it varies significantly and unpredictably over time, making accurate characterization with a limited number of measurements infeasible.
me: Experimental characterization of 160 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major manufacturers using repeated RDT measurements on the same rows over time. The study observes that the minimum RDT of a row only appears after up to 94,467 repeated measurements, with the minimum being 3.5x smaller than the observed maximum. Analysis covers the effects of chip density, technology node, data pattern, aggressor row open time, and temperature on RDT variability. Guardbanding and ECC (SECDED/Chipkill) approaches are evaluated as mitigations.
nv: First experimental demonstration that DRAM row RDT varies substantially and unpredictably over time (Variable Read Disturbance), fundamentally challenging the correctness of existing RowHammer characterization and mitigation strategies.

mx.other: Minimum RDT is 3.5x smaller than maximum observed; appears only after up to 94,467 measurements; 50% guardband causes ~45% performance loss

th: temporal variability of DRAM read disturbance thresholds

t: SPARK: Sparsity Aware, Low Area, Energy-Efficient, Near-memory Architecture for Accelerating Linear Programming Problems
pb: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and Linear Programming (LP) solvers run for tens of hours on large parallel computers because their sparse, branch-intensive algorithms are poorly matched to CPUs and GPUs. GPUs suffer from thread divergence on ILP branching and require frequent host interactions, while CPU solvers like Gurobi cannot meet real-time decision thresholds (seconds to minutes).
me: SPARK reconfigures the existing L1 cache in a CPU to act as a near-cache compute accelerator with ~1.4% area overhead. It integrates sparsity detection and sparsity-aware compute units near the cache to skip insignificant multiplications in sparse matrix operations, and exploits reuse patterns inherent to ILP algorithms (e.g., simplex pivots, branch-and-bound traversal) through a reuse-aware datapath. The architecture is reconfigurable to handle both sparse and dense ILPs and LPs without separate hardware.
nv: Near-L1-cache reconfiguration that enables sparsity-aware, reuse-aware computation for ILP/LP directly within the CPU pipeline at minimal area cost (~1.4% of a CPU).

mx.speedup: 15x over Zen3 CPU, 20x over V100 GPU (sparse ILP); 7-17x over CPU, 103-250x over GPU (sparse LP)
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 152x energy improvement over Zen3 CPU, 740x over V100 GPU (sparse ILP)
mx.area: ~1.4% of a CPU die area overhead

th: near-cache ILP/LP acceleration with sparsity awareness

t: Architecting Value Prediction around In-Order Execution
pb: In-order processors suffer from stalls when long-latency instructions block younger independent instructions from issuing, and the compiler cannot always find sufficient independent work to fill the pipeline. Conventional branch prediction techniques fail to resolve hard-to-predict (delinquent) branches quickly enough to prevent pipeline bubbles.
me: The paper integrates both address-based value prediction and direct value prediction into an in-order pipeline (based on a scaled-up CVA6 RISC-V core), exploiting the property that in-order execution allows aggressive value speculation without recovery penalties (a mispredicted value simply overwrites its slot when the real result arrives). A reworked cache hierarchy adds a fast first-level cache that can be written speculatively. A 32-entry scoreboard 4-issue in-order pipeline is augmented without full register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard handling.
nv: Demonstrating that in-order execution's deterministic instruction ordering enables penalty-free aggressive value speculation, achieving near-OOO performance without register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard resolution.

mx.speedup: 38.4% geomean IPC improvement over baseline in-order CVA6; 86.7% of OOO (32/16 ROB) gains; 46.3% of OOO (64/32 ROB) gains

th: value prediction for in-order processor performance

t: Machine Learning-Guided Memory Optimization for DLRM Inference on Tiered Memory
pb: Deep learning recommendation models (DLRMs) have embedding tables at terabyte scale that cannot fit in DRAM alone; tiered memory (DRAM + cheaper capacity tiers) is cost-effective but embedding access patterns have long and irregular reuse distances that defeat classical caching and prefetching heuristics.
me: RecMG uses separate ML models for caching and prefetching of embedding vectors. The caching model predicts which vectors have long reuse distances or few future reuses and should stay in fast memory. The prefetching model uses a novel differentiable loss function to narrow the search space for candidate vectors to prefetch, minimizing on-demand fetches. Data labeling is tailored to DLRM inference characteristics (sparse accesses, variable reuse distances). Both models operate at inference time to guide real-time placement decisions on tiered memory systems.
nv: A differentiable loss function for the prefetching ML model that narrows the prefetching candidate space and directly minimizes on-demand fetches for DLRM embedding vectors on tiered memory.

mx.speedup: Up to 43% reduction in end-to-end DLRM inference time
mx.other: On-demand fetch reduction: 2.2x vs temporal, 2.8x vs spatial, 1.5x vs ML-based prefetchers

th: ML-guided embedding placement for DLRM on tiered memory

t: FACIL: Flexible DRAM Address Mapping for SoC-PIM Cooperative On-device LLM Inference
pb: On-device LLM inference requires the same model weights to be accessed by both DRAM-based PIM units (for GEMV in the memory-bound decode phase) and SoC processors (for GEMM in the compute-bound prefill phase), but PIM-operable tensor layouts require different DRAM bank mappings from those preferred by SoC processors, creating costly re-layout overheads when switching between the two.
me: FACIL introduces a flexible DRAM address mapping scheme in the memory controller that assigns different DRAM address mappings to the page offset bits of each huge page. A user-level library determines the appropriate mapping for each tensor, allowing LLM weights to be placed in DRAM banks that are simultaneously PIM-operable and contiguously addressable by the SoC processor. This dual-mapping eliminates the need to copy or re-layout tensor data when switching between PIM-executed GEMV and SoC-executed GEMM operations.
nv: Per-huge-page configurable DRAM address mapping in the memory controller that allows the same physical tensor to be accessed coherently by both PIM hardware and SoC processors without data re-layout.

mx.speedup: 2.37x TTFT reduction (short conversation), 2.63x TTFT reduction (code autocompletion) over SoC-PIM baseline

th: flexible DRAM address mapping for cooperative SoC-PIM LLM inference

t: Delinquent Loop Pre-execution Using Predicated Helper Threads
pb: Helper-thread branch pre-execution fails when delinquent branches are control-dependent on other delinquent branches: prior work must branch-predict the first delinquent branch (b1) in the helper thread to decide whether to pre-execute the second (b2), merely shifting the misprediction bottleneck to the helper thread. Additionally, stores that both influence a delinquent branch and are control-dependent on it create a disambiguation problem in helper threads.
me: Phelps (Predicated Helper Threads) constructs a helper thread for each inner loop containing delinquent branches and unconditionally pre-executes all delinquent branches (including control-dependent ones) in every loop iteration. Per-branch queues are managed in lockstep with loop iterations, so the main thread can correctly consume or ignore b2 outcomes based on b1 results. Influential stores that are control-dependent on delinquent branches are predicated on those branch outcomes in the helper thread. A dual decoupled helper thread scheme handles outer-inner loop pairs with short/unpredictable inner-loop trip counts.
nv: Unconditional pre-execution of all delinquent branches (including control-dependent ones) via loop-iteration-lockstep per-branch queues, eliminating the need to predict delinquent branches within the helper thread itself.

mx.other: Not stated in abstract

th: predicated helper threads for delinquent branch pre-execution

t: Piccolo: Large-Scale Graph Processing with Fine-Grained in-Memory Scatter-Gather
pb: Graph processing requires irregular fine-grained random memory accesses incompatible with DDR memory access granularity, leading to massive bandwidth waste and cache capacity waste; existing approaches using graph tiling (maximizing on-chip reuse) or PIM (placing arithmetic near memory) each have limitations when implemented with DDR standards, and combining them is difficult.
me: Piccolo implements non-arithmetic function-in-memory focused specifically on fine-grained random scatter-gather operations in off-chip memory, avoiding expensive arithmetic units inside DRAM. The accelerator's cache and miss-handling architecture (MHA) are redesigned to work compatibly with in-memory scatter-gather, enabling both graph tiling (on-chip data reuse) and in-memory operations simultaneously. The scatter-gather function-in-memory reduces off-chip traffic without requiring the expensive multi-operation support that makes traditional PIM impractical.
nv: Placing only non-arithmetic scatter-gather function-in-memory rather than full arithmetic units, enabling cost-effective fine-grained random access reduction while preserving compatibility with graph tiling through a redesigned cache and MHA.

mx.speedup: Up to 3.28x (1.62x geomean) over prior graph processing accelerators

th: non-arithmetic in-memory scatter-gather for graph processing

t: Concord: Rethinking Distributed Coherence for Software Caches in Serverless Environments
pb: Serverless functions incur high latency from frequent global storage accesses; existing node-local caching schemes either restrict each data item to a single cache node (causing frequent remote reads) or allow multi-node replication but impose heavy coherence overhead, neither being optimal for serverless access patterns characterized by frequent reads, strong temporal locality, and few concurrent writers.
me: Concord implements a directory-based distributed software cache coherence protocol inspired by hardware cache coherence, adapted for serverless environments. It allows multiple replicas of the same data item across nodes and satisfies reads locally from any replica. To maintain coherence, a directory tracks replica locations and manages invalidation/update messages on writes. The protocol minimizes coherence traffic by exploiting serverless access patterns, reduces contention points in the directory, and handles node failures and frequent coherence domain changes (as serverless function instances spin up/down). Two additional capabilities are unlocked: transactional storage accesses and transparent data-aware function placement.
nv: A directory-based hardware-cache-coherence-inspired software coherence protocol tailored to serverless access patterns, enabling multi-node read replication with efficient invalidation while supporting transactional storage and data-aware placement.

mx.speedup: 2.4x execution speedup, 1.7x throughput improvement vs. state-of-the-art serverless caching on 16-node cluster
mx.other: Only 6.2MB (4.8% of application memory) overhead

th: hardware-inspired software cache coherence for serverless computing

t: IRIS: Unleashing ISP-Software Cooperation to Optimize the Machine Vision Pipeline
pb: Continuous Vision (CV) SoC pipelines capture entire scenes at uniform high resolution (e.g., 4K), wasting memory bandwidth and backend compute on low-information regions (sky, road) that do not require full-resolution processing, while the ISP discards intermediate computations (edge masks, motion vectors) that could guide resolution reduction.
me: IRIS augments the frontend ISP with three lightweight hardware units: (1) an IRIS Saliency Scorer that reuses ISP byproducts (the edge mask from Edge Enhancement and motion vectors from Temporal Denoising's Block Matching Algorithm) to compute a per-region saliency score (ISS = EDM + alpha * EDM * MM) without any new image analysis; (2) a Quad Unit that applies a hierarchical quadtree-like grouping (16x16, 32x32, 64x64 pixel regions) and compares maximum quadblock ISS to a backend-provided threshold to decide resolution; and (3) a Downsampling Unit that reduces selected quadblocks from 32x32 or 64x64 to 16x16 in-pipeline. The resulting mixed-resolution frame with a Region Resolution Map metadata is stored in the framebuffer. On the backend, for Vision Transformers IRIS feeds a mixed-resolution tokenizer (Quadformer-style), and for visual localization (ORB-SLAM3) IRIS enables an iterative feature extraction algorithm that processes regions in descending ISS order and stops on diminishing marginal feature increase. The ISP extension is validated as cycle-accurate RTL that never stalls the ISP pipeline.
nv: Repurposing already-computed ISP internal byproducts (edge mask from Edge Enhancement and motion vectors from Temporal Denoising) as a zero-additional-compute saliency scorer to drive per-region adaptive spatial resolution downsampling in the ISP pipeline before framebuffer write.

mx.speedup: Localization: 22.8% avg latency reduction, 10.5% tail latency reduction; Classification: 37.5% avg latency reduction, 9% tail latency reduction
mx.energy_or_tops_w: Localization: 22.5% energy reduction; Classification: 41.5% energy reduction
mx.area: Synthesized at 14nm with Synopsys; area overhead not quoted in headline but reported as negligible vs. ISP
mx.accuracy: ViT top-1 accuracy within 1% of baseline at ISS threshold 0.3; ORB-SLAM APE below 5mm at ISS=0.2, MFI=3%
mx.other: ~70% average image size reduction at threshold 0.5; 55% image size reduction at threshold 0.3

th: ISP-software cooperative adaptive resolution for mobile CV pipelines

t: To Cross, or Not to Cross Pages for Prefetching?
pb: L1D cache prefetchers operating with virtual addresses can issue prefetch requests across page boundaries, but whether page-cross prefetching is beneficial or harmful is workload- and phase-dependent, and existing prefetchers lack the intelligence to selectively enable or suppress these cross-page requests.
me: MOKA is a holistic framework for designing Page-Cross Filters that attach to existing L1D prefetchers. It combines three components: (i) hashed perceptron predictors using prefetcher-independent program features (PC, stride, memory access history) to estimate page-cross benefit, (ii) system-state-adaptive predictors that account for TLB pressure and MSHR occupancy, and (iii) a dynamic phase-switching scheme that periodically recalibrates filter decisions across changing execution phases. The resulting prototype filter, DRIPPER, is instantiated for Berti, IPCP, and BOP prefetchers without modifying their core logic.
nv: A systematic, predictor-agnostic framework (MOKA) for selectively gating page-cross prefetch requests using phase-adaptive hashed perceptron predictors that account for both program features and live system state.

mx.speedup: 1.7% over always-cross Berti (single-core); 2.5% over never-cross Berti; 2.0%/3.3% geomean on 8-core mixes vs always/never-cross

th: Selective page-cross prefetch filtering for L1D caches

t: Enterprise Class Modular Cache Hierarchy
pb: Enterprise mission-critical workloads demand cache hierarchies that deliver consistent low-latency performance at sustained processor utilization above 90% across diverse and highly virtualized workloads, while remaining extensible across processor generations and new technology insertions.
me: The IBM Telum and Telum II processors introduce a modular, horizontally federated cache hierarchy in which last-level cache slices are distributed across chiplets and interconnected through high-bandwidth on-chip links. An adaptive horizontal cache persistence algorithm dynamically adjusts which cache levels retain hot data across different access patterns and workload phases. The paper details how fetch events flow through this hierarchy and how cache size changes affect system-level performance, culminating in the Telum II design that simultaneously supports traditional enterprise workloads and generative AI inference.
nv: An industry-deployed modular and horizontally federated cache hierarchy with adaptive persistence algorithms designed for 90%+ sustained utilization in mission-critical enterprise and generative AI workloads.

mx.other: Sustained processor utilization >90%; specific speedup numbers not disclosed in abstract

th: Modular enterprise cache hierarchy for mission-critical and AI workloads

t: Reviving In-Storage Hardware Compression on ZNS SSDs through Host-SSD Collaboration
pb: Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs cannot benefit from traditional host-transparent in-storage hardware compression because the ZNS interface's sequential write constraint makes it impossible to locate variable-length compressed chunks and reclaim the space freed by compression without exposing this information to the host.
me: CCZNS (Collaborative Compression for ZNS) decouples compression execution from indexing by introducing a new ZNS interface extension where the SSD hardware performs compression but exposes chunk boundaries and offset metadata to the host rather than hiding them. The host (e.g., RocksDB with ZenFS) uses this metadata to manage address mapping and space reclamation, while the SSD accelerates the compression compute. A case study on RocksDB/ZenFS demonstrates how the host software is adapted to consume CCZNS metadata.
nv: Decoupling in-storage compression execution from index management via a host-SSD collaborative interface, which is the first solution to revive hardware compression on ZNS SSDs.

mx.other: Significantly outperforms existing system solutions (specific numbers not given in abstract)

th: Host-SSD collaborative hardware compression for ZNS SSDs

t: OASIS: Object-Aware Page Management for Multi-GPU Systems
pb: Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) in multi-GPU systems applies a single, application-object-agnostic page placement and migration policy to all data, failing to account for the fact that different data objects and different execution phases of the same object benefit from different page management strategies.
me: OASIS dynamically identifies application object access patterns at runtime by monitoring page-access counters and tracking object-level access behaviors across execution phases. Based on the detected patterns, it proactively assigns one of several page management policies—on-touch migration, access-counter-based migration, or duplication—to each object on a per-phase basis. The policy decision logic runs in software/hardware coordination and uses lightweight profiling to adapt to phase changes without manual programmer annotation.
nv: Runtime object-aware, phase-adaptive page management that automatically selects among migration and duplication policies per data object in multi-GPU UVM systems.

mx.speedup: 64% over on-touch migration; 35% over access-counter migration; 42% over duplication; 12% over GRIT

th: Object-aware adaptive page management for multi-GPU unified virtual memory

t: UniNDP: A Unified Compilation and Simulation Tool for Near DRAM Processing Architectures
pb: Existing simulators and compilers for Near DRAM Processing (NDP) architectures are designed for specific DRAM technologies and NDP configurations, preventing cross-architecture evaluation and optimal data placement and workload scheduling for machine learning workloads.
me: UniNDP proposes a unified tree-based NDP hardware abstraction and corresponding instruction set that spans multiple DRAM technologies and NDP configurations. A cycle-accurate, instruction-driven simulator tracks working status of memory elements and processing units at fine granularity to accurately evaluate hardware performance. An NDP compiler optimizes data partition, mapping, and workload scheduling across DRAM hierarchies, using a hardware status-guided search space pruning strategy and a fast performance predictor parameterized by DRAM timing parameters to improve compilation efficiency.
nv: A unified tree-based hardware abstraction with a matching instruction set that enables a single compilation and simulation framework to target diverse NDP architectures built on different DRAM technologies.

mx.speedup: 1.05-3.43x over existing mapping and compilation methods across multiple NDP architectures

th: unified compilation and simulation for near-DRAM processing architectures

t: I-DGNN: A Graph Dissimilarity-based Framework for Designing Scalable and Efficient DGNN Accelerators
pb: Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN) execution requires passing each graph snapshot through the entire DGNN pipeline from layer to layer, generating excessive intermediate data and off-chip memory access, even when consecutive snapshots differ only slightly.
me: I-DGNN proposes a one-pass DGNN computing model that extracts graph update as a chained matrix multiplication between evolving graphs through rigorous mathematical derivation, decoupling inter-snapshot computation from the full DGNN pipeline and expressing it as an independent kernel. A unified accelerator architecture is dynamically configured to support the computation characteristics of this model, providing improved data and pipeline parallelism. A new dataflow and mapping tailored to I-DGNN improves data locality for inter-kernel data across the DGNN pipeline. The framework reduces intermediate data movement across layers.
nv: Reformulating inter-snapshot DGNN computation as a standalone chained matrix multiplication kernel eliminates the need to route evolving graph data through the entire DGNN pipeline, cutting both compute redundancy and off-chip data movement.

mx.speedup: 65.9%, 71.1%, 58.8% execution time reduction vs. three state-of-the-art DGNN accelerators
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 88.4%, 87.0%, 85.9% energy efficiency improvement vs. three state-of-the-art DGNN accelerators

th: one-pass chained matrix multiplication for dynamic GNN acceleration

t: GoPIM: GCN-Oriented Pipeline Optimization for PIM Accelerators
pb: ReRAM-based PIM accelerators for GCN training suffer from severe pipeline underutilization due to skewed execution times across GCN stages (aggregation, combination) and skewed degree distributions of graph vertices, causing crossbar resource imbalance.
me: GoPIM employs an ML-based scheme that dynamically allocates ReRAM crossbar resources to the most needed pipeline stages to streamline overall execution and eliminate stage bottlenecks. A selective vertex updating technique interleaves vertex mapping across crossbars to evenly distribute vertices despite skewed degree distributions. These two mechanisms reduce overall execution time while maintaining accuracy. A practical architecture design for GoPIM is also provided.
nv: An ML-based crossbar resource allocation policy for GCN pipeline stages that adapts to runtime stage imbalance, combined with interleaved vertex mapping to handle skewed graph degree distributions in ReRAM PIM.

mx.speedup: up to 191x vs. state-of-the-art

th: pipeline-aware ReRAM PIM optimization for GCN training

t: Buffalo: Enabling Large-Scale GNN Training via Memory-Efficient Bucketization
pb: Training GNNs on large graphs using partitioning strategies causes a memory explosion problem driven by the long-tail degree distribution of graph nodes, and suffers from expensive graph partitioning, difficult memory estimation per partition, and slow data preparation (block generation).
me: Buffalo introduces node bucketization: a flexible mapping between nodes and partitions that addresses memory explosion by allowing nodes to be distributed to non-contiguous buckets based on degree, preventing any single partition from holding too many high-degree nodes. Fast graph partitioning is implemented based on node bucketing without requiring expensive global partitioning algorithms. A lightweight analytical model estimates memory consumption per partition before allocation, and graph sampling reduces block generation time during data preparation. Evaluation covers real-world billion-scale GNN datasets.
nv: Node bucketization that flexibly maps high-degree nodes across partitions to eliminate the memory explosion caused by long-tail degree distributions, enabling scalable large-scale GNN training within strict memory budgets.

mx.speedup: 70.9% end-to-end training time reduction on average vs. DGL, PyG, Betty
mx.other: enables training on billion-scale graphs that exceed GPU memory capacity

th: memory-efficient node bucketization for large-scale GNN training

t: Predicting DRAM-Caused Risky VMs in Large-Scale Clouds
pb: DRAM failures in large-scale clouds are currently mitigated at node granularity, requiring migration of all VMs on a node even when errors affect only a small fraction of the memory address space. This coarse-grained approach consumes excessive resources and causes unnecessary VM disruptions.
me: Pegasus introduces an Error-VM mapping framework that correlates DRAM ECC error addresses to specific VM memory regions using address space management metadata. A predictor combines ECC correction event features with spatio-temporal clustering features to identify VMs whose working sets overlap with DRAM regions exhibiting uncorrectable error risk. The system operates at VM granularity rather than DIMM/node granularity, enabling selective migration of only at-risk VMs.
nv: First VM-level DRAM failure prediction system that maps DRAM error addresses to specific virtual machines, enabling fine-grained proactive migration rather than whole-node migration.

mx.other: >70% lower migration cost vs. node-level; >10% fewer VM crashes; deployed on 300,000+ production nodes

th: VM-granularity DRAM failure prediction for cloud reliability

t: RpcNIC: Enabling Efficient Datacenter RPC Offloading on PCIe-attached SmartNICs
pb: RPC processing has become a dominant datacenter tax in microservice/serverless environments, but existing RPC accelerators either integrate logic into the CPU or use specialized low-latency interconnects unavailable in commodity servers, preventing broad deployment.
me: RpcNIC is a software-hardware co-designed SmartNIC on Xilinx U280 FPGA using three techniques to mitigate PCIe overhead: (1) a target-aware deserializer that batches cross-PCIe writes on SmartNIC SRAM using compacted hardware data structures to reduce PCIe transaction count; (2) a memory-affinity CPU-SmartNIC collaborative serializer that trades host memory copies for slow PCIe transfers, keeping data on the host side for NUMA-affine access; and (3) an automatic field update mechanism that dynamically reconfigures RPC kernel schema encoding to minimize redundant PCIe traversals when application schemas change.
nv: A three-pronged PCIe-aware co-design that makes commodity PCIe-attached SmartNICs competitive with specialized low-latency interconnect RPC accelerators for datacenter workloads.

mx.speedup: 2.3x lower RPC layer processing time vs. comparable RPC accelerator; 2.6x achievable throughput in end-to-end cloud workload

th: PCIe-aware SmartNIC hardware-software co-design for datacenter RPC offload

t: Gemina: A Coordinated and High-Performance Memory Deduplication Engine
pb: Memory deduplication (via KSM) eliminates duplicate pages but forces huge pages to split into 4KB base pages, degrading TLB hit rates and memory access performance by up to 43%; asynchronous huge page promotion cannot recover this loss because deduplication breaks the uniformity of page attributes required for promotion.
me: Gemina coordinates huge page management with memory deduplication through three components: (1) a fine-grained detector that separately classifies pages by both redundancy and access hotness to decouple deduplication decisions from page-size decisions; (2) a distributor that conservatively processes pages to avoid frequent hot/cold and size-class switches; and (3) an adapter that reorganizes memory layout to enable fast base-to-huge-page conversion. Together, these components preserve huge page availability by selectively deferring or avoiding deduplication of hot pages while still capturing most memory savings.
nv: Jointly optimizing memory deduplication and huge page management through a coordinated three-component system that preserves huge page promotability while retaining near-full deduplication savings.

mx.other: 96.1% of KSM memory savings retained; 43.1% memory access performance improvement vs. naive KSM-based deduplication

th: Coordinated huge-page-aware memory deduplication to recover TLB performance

t: SkyByte: Architecting an Efficient Memory-Semantic CXL-based SSD with OS and Hardware Co-design
pb: CXL-based SSDs enable byte-granular memory expansion at low cost, but suffer from long flash access latency, unpredictable garbage collection stalls, and a fundamental mismatch between byte-granular CXL access and page-granular flash I/O that wastes significant bandwidth.
me: SkyByte co-designs the host OS and SSD controller with three mechanisms: (1) opportunistic OS context switches triggered when the processor detects long CXL-SSD access delays, hiding latency via thread-level parallelism; (2) a cacheline-level write log and page-level data cache within SSD controller DRAM that coalesces byte-granular writes and performs data merging at log cleaning time to reduce flash I/O traffic; and (3) adaptive page migration that promotes hot CXL-SSD pages to fast host DRAM based on access frequency. The combination reduces both stall cycles and unnecessary flash I/O amplification.
nv: OS-level opportunistic context switching combined with a two-tier SSD controller DRAM structure (cacheline write log + page cache) that bridges the byte-granular CXL access and page-granular flash I/O mismatch.

mx.speedup: 6.11x over current CXL-based SSD
mx.other: 23.08x reduction in flash chip I/O traffic; achieves 75% of ideal unlimited-DRAM performance

th: OS-hardware co-design for byte-granular CXL-SSD memory expansion efficiency

t: MeHyper: Accelerating Hypergraph Neural Networks by Exploring Implicit Dataflows
pb: Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) based on hyperedge-centric dataflow independently process vertex and hyperedge aggregation tasks, causing significant computational redundancy from recalculating shared information (intermediate feature values) across these tasks.
me: MeHyper introduces a microedge concept that captures fine-grained shared information between aggregation tasks, replacing the hyperedge-centric model with a microedge-centric dataflow that processes shared information once and distributes it to all dependent tasks. The execution follows a Read-Process-Activate-Generate model optimized for parallel microedge task processing. The hardware accelerator features a decoupled pipeline for improved computational parallelism and a hierarchical feature management strategy that partitions on-chip memory across feature granularities to reduce off-chip DRAM accesses for the large intermediate feature vectors generated during microedge aggregation.
nv: First identification and exploitation of implicit dataflow dependencies within HGNNs via the microedge abstraction, eliminating inter-task computational redundancy across vertex and hyperedge aggregation.

mx.speedup: 1032.23x over PyG-CPU; 10.51x over HyperGef (GPU)
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 1169.03x energy efficiency over PyG-CPU; 9.96x over HyperGef

th: Microedge-centric dataflow accelerator for redundancy-free HGNN computation

t: Criticality-Aware Instruction-Centric Bandwidth Partitioning for Data Center Applications
pb: Co-locating latency-critical (LC) and best-effort (BE) tasks on shared datacenter nodes causes memory bandwidth contention that results in priority inversion, where BE tasks monopolize bandwidth and cause LC tasks to violate quality-of-service (QoS) requirements.
me: Pivot is a bandwidth partitioning system that prioritizes LC memory accesses at every component along the full memory path (L1/L2/L3 caches, DRAM controller) rather than at a single bottleneck point. Critically, Pivot selectively prioritizes only performance-critical loads—those causing long stalls on the re-order buffer (ROB)—rather than all LC accesses. A two-phase profiling technique identifies these critical loads offline with minimal runtime overhead: Phase 1 profiles whole-execution hit/miss behavior per load PC, and Phase 2 uses those profiles to tag critical loads for hardware prioritization during production runs.
nv: Instruction-centric identification of ROB-stalling critical loads combined with full-memory-path prioritization, avoiding bandwidth waste from protecting non-critical LC accesses.

mx.other: Up to 34.5% effective machine utilization improvement; up to 2.76x BE throughput improvement vs. state-of-the-art

th: Criticality-aware instruction-level memory bandwidth partitioning for LC/BE co-location

t: From Optimal to Practical: Efficient Micro-op Cache Replacement Policies for Data Center Applications
pb: Data center applications suffer frequent micro-op (uop) cache misses because no effective uop-cache-specific replacement policy exists; the uop cache has fundamentally different cost characteristics from conventional caches (variable and disproportional miss costs, partial hits), making standard policies like LRU and even Belady's algorithm suboptimal.
me: FLACK is introduced as a near-optimal offline replacement policy that accounts for uop cache-specific properties: variable miss costs (due to disproportional re-fetch penalties) and partial hits (when only some micro-ops of an instruction group are cached). FLACK substantially outperforms Belady's algorithm, establishing a new uop-cache-specific optimality bound. FURBYS is then designed as a practical online policy that mimics FLACK via profile-guided methods, using three components: (1) whole-execution hit/miss profiles per static instruction, (2) detection of locally/transiently hot data, and (3) selective ignorance of entries with profiled low hit rates during replacement decisions.
nv: FLACK—a near-optimal offline uop cache replacement algorithm that accounts for variable miss costs and partial hits, surpassing Belady's algorithm and providing a new theoretical bound for practical policy design.

mx.speedup: 3.10% performance-per-watt improvement for CPU core
mx.other: 14.34% average miss reduction over LRU (1.84x over state-of-the-art); FLACK: 30.21% average miss reduction bound, 4.46% greater than Belady

th: Near-optimal uop cache replacement policy design from theoretical bound to practical profile-guided implementation

t: ANVIL: An In-Storage Accelerator for Name-Value Data Stores
pb: Large-scale name-value pair (NVP) lookups saturate both external and internal SSD bandwidth because every NVP must be sent to the host CPU to check for a name match. Existing NVP optimizations are limited to a single data store format, leaving the broad heterogeneity of NVP encodings unaddressed.
me: ANVIL implements in-storage processing by pushing name-match logic directly into the NAND flash chips of a conventional SSD. Rather than streaming all key-value data to the host, ANVIL performs name-match filtering inside the storage device, discarding non-matching NVPs before they traverse the SSD-host interface. The system is designed as an end-to-end in-storage accelerator that supports multiple NVP formats (arrays, dictionaries, key-value stores, data mining structures) through a unified near-storage computation model.
nv: ANVIL is the first end-to-end in-storage system that accelerates a broad range of NVP data store formats by filtering non-matching names inside NAND flash chips, eliminating unnecessary host-bound I/O.

mx.speedup: 4.0x (database), 25x (analytics), 14.6% (graph processing) over conventional SSD
mx.other: Reduced disk I/O and metadata overhead

th: In-storage near-data processing for key-value workloads

t: Leveraging control-flow similarity to reduce branch predictor cold effects in microservices
pb: Microservices suffer from severe branch mispredictions due to cold branch predictor state when cores are shared across interleaved service invocations or power-gated between requests. This cold-start effect degrades tail latency under strict SLA constraints.
me: The authors propose Similarity-based Branch Prediction (SBP), a hybrid predictor that augments conventional history-based and static-hint predictors with a similarity component (CHESS). CHESS encodes the control flow of prior request executions into a compact reference execution trace, then identifies branches that are hard to predict via conventional means and redirects them to the similarity predictor. The similarity predictor leverages dynamic control-flow reconvergence analysis to replay past execution paths for matching current requests, requiring only 18.1 KB of additional storage.
nv: CHESS exploits inter-request control-flow similarity in microservices—encoding prior execution traces as reference paths—to warm-start branch prediction for cold-predictor scenarios without requiring actual predictor state persistence.

mx.speedup: Within 95% of warm baseline performance
mx.accuracy: 94% branch MPKI reduction vs. cold predictor; 78% vs. state-of-the-art warm predictor
mx.other: 18.1 KB additional storage overhead

th: Cold-start branch prediction using inter-request control-flow similarity for microservices

t: Folded Banks: 3D-Stacked HBM Design for Fine-Grained Random-Access Bandwidth
pb: HBM has seen substantial improvements in sequential (peak) bandwidth across generations but irregular/random-access bandwidth has stagnated, limiting performance for applications with non-sequential memory access patterns such as graph analytics, recommendation, and sparse workloads.
me: Folded Banks (FB-HBM) redistributes DRAM bank subarrays by folding them across multiple dies in a 3D stack and relocating command/control logic and global sense amplifiers to a new dedicated base layer implemented in a logic process. Intra-bank column select lines (CSLs) and master data lines (MDLs) are routed vertically through thin-pitch through-silicon vias (TSVs) and hybrid bonds, dramatically reducing RC power losses from long horizontal routing. Self-timed sense amplifiers eliminate the need for costly dummy subarrays, further reducing power and area on the DRAM dies.
nv: Redistributing bank subarrays across stacked dies with vertical TSV/hybrid-bond routing and a dedicated logic base layer eliminates the power and area penalties of conventional horizontal global wiring in DRAM, enabling fine-grained random-access activation at lower energy.

mx.other: 6.4x increase in sequential bandwidth over two HBM generations cited as baseline gap; random-access improvement metric not quantified in abstract

th: 3D-stacked HBM bank folding for fine-grained random-access bandwidth

t: Avalanche: Optimizing Cache Utilization via Matrix Reordering for Sparse Matrix Multiplication Accelerator
pb: Sparse Matrix Multiplication (SpMM) accelerators suffer from poor on-chip memory utilization due to irregular memory access patterns; existing designs fail to cache both input matrices efficiently, leading to redundant DRAM accesses and low throughput.
me: Avalanche applies three complementary techniques: (1) Mat-Reorder reorders columns of matrix B to maximize data locality and enable early completion of row computations in matrix A; (2) DP-Evict (Dead-Product Early Eviction) immediately evicts fully-computed intermediate products from on-chip SRAM to reclaim capacity; (3) RM-Caching (Reuse Distance-Aware Matrix Caching) prioritizes retention of matrix B elements with short reuse distances in the on-chip cache. Together these techniques keep both operand matrices resident in a 6.15 mm2 chip with minimal spill-to-DRAM.
nv: Column reordering of the sparse input matrix (Mat-Reorder) to align non-zero access patterns with on-chip cache capacity, enabling simultaneous caching of both operand matrices.

mx.speedup: 1.97x average over state-of-the-art SpMM accelerator

th: on-chip cache optimization for sparse matrix multiplication

t: Enabling Ahead Prediction with Practical Energy Constraints
pb: Branch predictors require multiple pipeline cycles to produce a prediction, causing a latency penalty; ahead prediction solves this by starting early but must consider all 2^N possible histories for the N intermediate branches, increasing energy by 14.6x and making the approach impractical.
me: The authors observe that most of the 2^N possible intermediate branch-direction combinations never actually occur at runtime; only one or two patterns are observed in practice. They modify the TAGE predictor to track and eliminate non-materializing history patterns, reducing the number of parallel prediction paths that must be evaluated. This allows the ahead predictor to operate with only 1.5x energy overhead instead of the previously assumed 14.6x, while delivering 4.4% IPC improvement.
nv: Observation that intermediate branch history patterns rarely materialize reduces the effective branching factor of ahead prediction from exponential to near-constant, making practical ahead prediction feasible.

mx.speedup: 4.4% performance improvement

th: energy-efficient ahead branch prediction

t: REIS: A High-Performance and Energy-Efficient Retrieval System with In-Storage Processing
pb: The retrieval stage of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a throughput bottleneck because Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) on large embedding databases incurs massive data movement between host and storage; existing In-Storage Processing (ISP) approaches use storage-agnostic ANNS algorithms, do not accelerate the subsequent data-fetch step, and require heavy SSD hardware modifications.
me: REIS co-designs the ANNS algorithm with ISP hardware inside the storage system to avoid host-storage data movement. It adopts an ISP-tailored ANNS algorithm that exploits the internal bandwidth and parallelism of NAND flash controllers without large hardware modifications. REIS additionally accelerates the data-retrieval step for items selected by ANNS, overlapping fetch and search computations. The system is designed to minimize changes to storage hardware while maximizing throughput.
nv: ISP-tailored ANNS algorithm that co-designs the search procedure with the flash storage controller's internal architecture, simultaneously accelerating both vector search and subsequent data retrieval without significant hardware modification.

mx.other: High performance and energy efficiency claimed; specific numbers not reported in abstract

th: in-storage processing for RAG retrieval acceleration

t: Ecco: Improving Memory Bandwidth and Capacity for LLMs via Entropy-Aware Cache Compression
pb: LLM inference is severely memory-bandwidth-bound and memory-capacity-constrained due to large KV caches and weight tensors; the KV cache alone can consume 72.7% of GPU memory. Existing quantization schemes (AWQ, SmoothQuant, Quarot) reduce storage but introduce high runtime decompression overheads that negate bandwidth savings or compromise accuracy.
me: Ecco integrates a parallel compressor/decompressor pair between the GPU L2 cache and HBM. Weights and KV cache are compressed 4x using group-wise (group size 128) non-uniform k-means quantization with 64 shared k-means patterns per tensor, plus clipped/padded Huffman coding with 4 per-pattern codebooks; activations use a simpler 2x uniform INT8 scheme. The 4x decompressor deploys 64 parallel Huffman sub-decoders operating on overlapping 15-bit windows of the 512-bit compressed block, fused with a 6-stage tree-based concatenator and 128 parallel mappers. The compressor uses a bitonic sorter for scale factor / outlier extraction and a min/max fitness score to select among 16 shared k-means patterns online. Both components are replicated 20x to match the 5120 B/cycle L2 throughput, implemented in 28nm (scaled to 7nm).
nv: A parallel multi-stage Huffman decoder that breaks the sequential decoding barrier using 64 overlapping sub-decoders fused with a tree concatenation stage, achieving two-orders-of-magnitude latency reduction and GPU L2-comparable throughput for a lossy, entropy-aware compression scheme.

mx.speedup: 2.9x over TensorRT FP16 (avg), 2.9x over AWQ, 2.4x over Olive, 1.9x over SmoothQuant on LLaMA-13B decode
mx.area: 5.11 mm2 total hardware addition on A100 (826 mm2 die), <1% area overhead; 7.36 W power (<10% of A100 idle power)
mx.accuracy: LLaMA2-7B perplexity 5.65 (W4A8KV4) vs AWQ 5.83; outperforms all baselines on LLaMA/LLaMA2 7B-70B
mx.other: 4x memory capacity enlargement for weights and KV cache; 2x for activations

th: entropy-aware cache compression for LLM inference on GPU

t: MagiCache: A Virtual In-Cache Computing Engine
pb: Array-level in-cache computing architectures dedicate entire cache arrays as compute arrays, leaving most computing lines idle at runtime while the non-computing arrays absorb large bursty memory accesses—both causing severe on-chip capacity loss and high data movement latency for data-parallel applications.
me: MagiCache introduces cacheline-level in-cache computing: each cache array can dynamically configure individual rows as either computing lines or cachelines with negligible hardware overhead. A virtual engine monitors runtime computation and storage requirements and dynamically reallocates rows within each array between compute and cache roles via cacheline-level space management. An instruction chaining technique enables asynchronous execution of computing arrays, overlapping bursty HBM/DRAM access latency with ongoing computation through pipelined, out-of-order scheduling of memory requests and compute operations.
nv: A virtual in-cache computing engine that performs cacheline-granularity dynamic allocation of SRAM rows between compute and cache roles, eliminating the fixed capacity loss of array-level in-cache architectures while hiding bursty memory access latency via instruction chaining.

mx.speedup: 1.19–1.61x over state-of-the-art in-cache computing architectures

th: Cacheline-granularity virtual in-cache computing with dynamic row allocation

t: Rethinking Prefetching for Intermittent Computing
pb: Conventional hardware prefetchers are energy-wasteful on batteryless energy harvesting systems (EHSs) because they aggressively fetch cache lines that are lost on power failure before any hit, wasting harvested energy. Frequent outages on EHSs mean that prefetched data that is never accessed before the next power loss represents pure energy overhead.
me: IPEX (Intermittence-aware Prefetching EXtension) is an add-on layer that wraps existing prefetchers on EHSs without replacing them. It tracks which prefetched cache blocks receive a hit before a power failure and suppresses future prefetches of lines that historically go unused ('useless prefetches'). Additionally, IPEX monitors harvested energy levels to predict imminent outages and dynamically throttles the prefetch degree at that moment, targeting only blocks likely to be accessed before power loss.
