The result is that harvested energy is redirected from futile prefetches toward productive forward execution progress.
nv: IPEX is the first prefetch extension that actively suppresses prefetches based on predicted power-failure timing and historical usefulness tracking, converting energy that would be wasted on lost cache lines into forward progress.

mx.speedup: 1.09x average (up to 1.23x) vs conventional prefetcher
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 7.86% avg energy reduction (up to 21.64%) vs conventional prefetcher

th: energy-aware prefetch suppression for intermittent computing

t: Heliostat: Harnessing Ray Tracing Accelerators for Page Table Walks
pb: GPU virtual memory page table walks are a critical performance bottleneck as workloads with large address spaces saturate the GPU Memory Management Unit (GMMU), which cannot be straightforwardly scaled without significant area and power overhead. Existing approaches focus on better utilizing fixed translation bandwidth rather than fundamentally increasing it.
me: Heliostat repurposes the underutilized ray tracing accelerators (RTAs) already present in modern GPUs to perform page table walks, exploiting the structural similarity between ray-box/triangle intersection traversal and radix-tree page table traversal. The design maps page-table-walk state machines onto RTA traversal units to increase total translation bandwidth without adding dedicated GMMU hardware. Heliostat+ extends this by proactively performing predicted future address translations (prefetch-style speculation on the translation path) to further reduce effective TLB-miss latency. This approach democratizes RTA use across all workloads, not just ray-traced rendering.
nv: Heliostat is the first design to repurpose ray tracing accelerators as page table walk engines, leveraging the structural isomorphism between BVH tree traversal and radix page table walks to increase GPU address translation bandwidth at 1.53% the area and 5.8% the power of an equivalently overprovisioned GMMU.

mx.speedup: 1.93x over baseline GPU; 1.92x over SoTA 1; 1.66x over SoTA 2; Heliostat+ further 1.23x over Heliostat

th: repurposing ray tracing accelerators for GPU page table walks

t: Magellan: A High-Performance Loop-Guided Prefetcher for Indirect Memory Access
pb: Graph analytics and sparse linear algebra applications rely heavily on indirect memory access (IMA), where pointer-chasing through irregular data structures causes frequent high-latency DRAM accesses due to poor temporal and spatial locality. Existing hardware and software prefetchers for IMA target narrow access patterns and struggle with complex nested-loop IMA patterns in sparse workloads.
me: Magellan is a compiler-based software prefetcher that constructs dependence graphs across loop levels to detect complex multi-level IMA patterns. It captures inner-outer loop semantics to schedule prefetches for both current and future loop iterations, inserting prefetch instructions ahead of the load chain. The compiler analysis extracts the indirection chains (e.g., A[B[i]]) across nested loop boundaries and emits prefetch instructions with appropriate software distances derived from loop trip counts and memory latency estimates.
nv: Magellan is the first software prefetcher to model cross-loop-level dependence graphs and leverage inner-outer loop semantics to prefetch across nested IMA patterns, enabling coverage of access patterns that prior single-level approaches miss.

mx.speedup: 1.14x average, up to 1.41x over best existing IMA software prefetcher
mx.other: 25% cache miss reduction, 14% dynamic instruction count reduction

th: compiler-guided software prefetching for irregular memory access

t: NUPEA: Optimizing Critical Loads on Spatial Dataflow Architectures via Non-Uniform Processing-Element Access
pb: On large spatial dataflow architectures (SDAs) where program instructions are distributed across a fabric of processing elements (PEs), some PEs are physically closer to memory than others, creating non-uniform data access latencies (NUPEA). Existing approaches focused on NUMA-style data placement, which is complex and often ineffective when critical data is hard to identify statically.
me: NUPEA observes that on large SDAs, placing critical load instructions on PEs physically close to memory reduces data movement costs. The authors implement architecture extensions and compiler optimizations for NUPEA on the Monaco SDA (by Efficient Computer) and its effcc compiler. The compiler identifies critical loads via dependence analysis and maps them to near-memory PEs, while the architecture exposes PE-to-memory proximity information to the compiler. This contrasts with NUMA where data is moved closer to fixed PEs.
nv: NUPEA inverts the data-centric NUMA paradigm: rather than moving data near compute, it places compute (load instructions) near memory on spatial dataflow architectures, which is more tractable for compiler analysis.

mx.speedup: 28% avg over uniform-PE-access SDA; 20% avg over UPEA+NUMA SDA

th: instruction placement near memory on spatial dataflow architectures

t: WarmCache: Exploiting STT-RAM Cache for Low-Power Intermittent Systems
pb: Energy harvesting systems (EHS) suffer from compulsory cache misses after power failures because volatile SRAM caches lose all data across power outages, forcing cold-start cache rebuilding on each power restoration. Existing non-volatile cache designs impose high write energy and latency overhead.
me: WarmCache uses an STT-RAM cache with relaxed thermal stability (reduced retention time) tuned so cache contents survive typical power outage durations without requiring full non-volatile persistence. The compiler partitions the program into regions and performs region-level error correction: at each region boundary, updated cache lines are scrubbed and any multi-bit retention errors trigger re-execution of that region. A region formation technique via stitching (combining short regions) and splitting (dividing long regions) aligns region boundaries with the STT-RAM scrubbing interval.
nv: Using relaxed-retention STT-RAM (not fully non-volatile) to preserve cache warmth across power outages, combined with compiler-driven region-level error correction to handle retention failures without write-back overhead.

mx.speedup: 1.3-1.4x over state-of-the-art EHS cache design

th: Relaxed-retention STT-RAM cache for intermittent energy-harvesting systems

t: SEAL: A Single-Event Architecture for In-Sensor Visual Localization
pb: Traditional binary-encoded image sensors generate large data volumes that create energy and latency bottlenecks during transfer, storage, and processing for visual localization tasks such as keypoint detection and tracking. Moving these operations off-sensor to a host processor adds significant latency and energy cost.
me: SEAL introduces delay-based (temporal) codes at the pixel array level, replacing binary encoding with analog-to-time converters (ATCs) that represent pixel values as pulse delays (race logic). A temporal processor co-designed with the ATCs implements keypoint detection and tracking using race logic's single-wire-per-variable, single-event-per-wire policy, maximizing energy and area efficiency. A heavily quantized frontend processor then processes temporal outputs before the sensor-processor interface, enabling in-sensor VIO pipeline stages.
nv: End-to-end in-sensor localization pipeline built on delay-based (race logic) encoding instead of binary encoding, enabling keypoint detection and tracking within the pixel sensor itself using fully digital CMOS circuits.

mx.speedup: 16-61x latency reduction for keypoint detection and tracking vs. software baseline on host processor
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 7x energy reduction vs. standard digital pixel sensor
mx.accuracy: ATE RMSE changes: -1.0 cm (HybVIO), +0.3 cm (VINS-Mono) on EuRoC

th: In-sensor visual localization via delay-based race logic encoding

t: InfiniMind: A Learning-Optimized Large-Scale Brain-Computer Interface
pb: Deploying continual learning on NVM-assisted implanted BCI systems incurs excessive write overhead on non-volatile memory, drastically reducing NVM endurance (lifetime) and causing performance bottlenecks that make continual adaptation to non-stationary neural signals impractical.
me: InfiniMind proposes four NVM-write optimization schemes implemented in a memory controller: (1) update filtering exploits sparse and recurring nature of BCI signals to skip unnecessary writes; (2) delta buffering uses temporal locality in neural signals to accumulate deltas and batch NVM writes; (3) out-of-place flushing packs multiple sub-page updates into single page writes to reduce write amplification; and (4) waveform compression exploits structural characteristics of neural waveforms to reduce data volume. These are integrated as a memory controller layer on top of an NVM-assisted BCI system running continual learning algorithms.
nv: A memory controller combining four complementary NVM-write optimizations tailored to the sparse, temporally-local, and structurally-regular characteristics of BCI neural signals.

mx.speedup: 5.39x performance improvement
mx.other: 23.52x NVM lifetime extension over state-of-the-art NVM-assisted BCI system

th: NVM write optimization for continual learning in implanted BCI systems

t: UPP: Universal Predicate Pushdown to Smart Storage
pb: Existing in-storage processing (ISP) solutions only support simple operators (equality, range comparisons) on fixed-length columns, leaving modern analytical queries that use complex operators and diverse data formats unaccelerated. There is no flexible ISP mechanism that can handle arbitrary filter predicates used in production databases.
me: UPP defines a compact, purpose-built ISA for predicate pushdown that is separate from individual operator implementations. The database software layer recognizes filter predicates, compiles them to UPP-compliant instructions, and ships them to an FPGA (SmartSSD) where bitwise comparison execution leverages lightweight metadata to evaluate predicates directly in storage without reformatting data. The hardware/software co-design avoids changing input data formats on disk while enabling flexible predicate evaluation through this instruction-level abstraction.
nv: A compact ISA tailored explicitly for predicate pushdown allows the database to compile arbitrary, complex filter predicates into storage-executable instructions, achieving generality that prior ISP designs relying on hardwired operator logic cannot.

mx.speedup: 1.2–7.9x end-to-end Spark query speedup on TPC-H 100 GB

th: flexible ISA for in-storage predicate evaluation

t: DX100: Programmable Data Access Accelerator for Indirection
pb: Indirect memory accesses (A[B[i]] patterns) in scientific computing, graph analytics, and database workloads cause severe DRAM bandwidth underutilization because DRAM controllers have only a 32–128 request window to reorder commands, while the dependency chains of indirect loads limit the memory-level parallelism achievable by conventional cores. Prior prefetchers and fetcher units improve latency but do not reorder, coalesce, or interleave accesses for bandwidth efficiency.
me: DX100 is a programmable, memory-mapped accelerator shared across CPU cores that offloads bulk indirect and streaming memory operations. An 8-instruction ISA supports indirect loads/stores/RMWs, streaming loads/stores, ALU operations, and range-loop fusion. The Indirect Access unit uses a Row Table (BCAM + SRAM) to reorder up to 16K indices per tile for DRAM row-buffer hit maximization, a Word Table for coalescing redundant column accesses, and a Request Generator that interleaves requests across DRAM channels and bank groups. Streaming accesses go to the LLC via Cache Interface; indirect accesses bypass the cache hierarchy and inject directly into DRAM controllers, with a Coherency Agent maintaining cache coherence by snooping directories during the fill stage. An MLIR-based compiler (using Polygeist for C/C++ lowering) automatically detects indirect accesses, performs loop tiling, hoists bulk operations, and emits DX100 API calls—covering over 99% of graph frontier nodes across evaluated benchmarks.
nv: DX100 uses a large (16K-entry) hardware Row Table that reorders the full tile of indirect indices before issuing DRAM requests, providing 500x more reordering visibility than DRAM controller request buffers (32 entries) and achieving near-peak DRAM bandwidth utilization regardless of index distribution.

mx.speedup: 2.6x over 4-core multicore baseline; 2.0x over DMP indirect prefetcher (geometric mean, 12 benchmarks)
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 3.6x core instruction reduction (energy proxy); 777 mW power at 28nm
mx.area: 4.06 mm^2 at 28nm (~1.5 mm^2 at 14nm, 3.7% of 4-core processor area)
mx.other: 3.9x average DRAM bandwidth utilization improvement; 2.7x row-buffer hit rate increase; 12.1x DRAM controller request buffer occupancy increase; 6.1x cache MPKI reduction

th: programmable bulk-indirect-access accelerator for DRAM bandwidth optimization

t: EOD: Enabling Low Latency GNN Inference via Near-Memory Concatenate Aggregation
pb: Real-time GNN inference for online services requires an inductive setup where the system must first prepare the computational graph and node features before executing inference, with this preparation step dominating end-to-end latency. The neighborhood explosion problem causes exponential growth in memory access and computation as the number of GNN layers increases.
me: EOD co-designs algorithm and hardware to tackle both challenges. On the algorithmic side, it introduces a precomputation method for training nodes that converts exponential neighborhood aggregation to linear complexity, and a concatenated Zero-Value Compression (ZVC) scheme to compact the stored precomputed hidden features. On the hardware side, EOD implements a Near-Memory Processing (NMP) architecture that performs aggregation directly on ZVC-compressed, concatenated feature data without decompressing to host memory, exploiting the high internal memory bandwidth to eliminate the PCIe/host-memory bottleneck during the preparation stage.
nv: A concatenated ZVC compression format co-designed with a dedicated NMP aggregation engine that operates natively on compressed GNN features, eliminating the host-side memory access bottleneck entirely.

mx.speedup: 981.1x geomean aggregation speedup over baseline; 17.9x geomean end-to-end speedup over GPU baseline; up to 74.3x end-to-end speedup

th: Near-memory GNN aggregation with compressed feature precomputation

t: NMP-PaK: Near-Memory Processing Acceleration of Scalable De Novo Genome Assembly
pb: De novo genome assembly using De Bruijn graph (DBG) algorithms is both memory-latency-bound and memory-footprint-intensive: processing 10% of the human genome (38.3 GB input) requires 528 GB of DRAM, and the Iterative Compaction step—which dominates 48% of runtime—achieves only 2.5% of available memory bandwidth due to fine-grained, irregular access patterns across large, dynamic MacroNode data structures.
me: NMP-PaK places pipelined systolic Processing Elements (PEs) inside DIMM buffer chips (channel-level NMP) to exploit high internal memory bandwidth and reduce data movement latency. Each PE implements a 3-stage pipeline (Invalidation Check, TransferNode Extraction, Routing and Update) operating at MacroNode granularity, with an intra-DIMM crossbar switch and an inter-DIMM network bridge routing TransferNodes between PEs. Software optimizations complement the hardware: customized batch processing divides the genome into 10% batches to reduce peak memory footprint by 14x, pointer-aliasing deduplication eliminates redundant MacroNode copies, and a hybrid CPU-NMP strategy offloads large MacroNodes (>1 KB) to the CPU to avoid PE buffer oversizing and workload imbalance.
nv: Channel-level NMP with pipelined systolic PEs co-designed specifically for the MacroNode data structure of DBG assembly, enabling parallel MacroNode-granular Iterative Compaction with inter-DIMM TransferNode routing and a hybrid CPU-NMP offload policy for irregular outliers.

mx.speedup: 16x over CPU baseline; 5.7x over GPU (A100); 8.3x throughput vs PaKman supercomputer under same resources
mx.accuracy: 14x memory footprint reduction; 2.4x reduction in memory operations
mx.other: Memory bandwidth utilization: 44% (NMP-PaK) vs 6.5% (CPU baseline)

th: Channel-level NMP acceleration of De Bruijn graph genome assembly

t: LIA: A Single-GPU LLM Inference Acceleration with Cooperative AMX-Enabled CPU-GPU Computation and CXL Offloading
pb: Single-GPU LLM inference is constrained by GPU memory capacity, forcing either expensive multi-GPU deployments or frequent CPU-GPU transfers over slow PCIe, which bottleneck both latency and throughput.
me: LIA is a single-GPU LLM inference framework that systematically offloads matrix computations to AMX-enabled CPUs (4th-gen Sapphire Rapids and 6th-gen Granite Rapids Xeon), reducing CPU-GPU transfers by keeping model parameters near the CPU. LIA introduces a memory-offloading policy that integrates CXL memory (as an affordable DRAM extension) with DDR memory to expand effective model capacity for throughput-oriented batch workloads. The system partitions transformer layer computations between CPU and GPU based on runtime latency/throughput objectives, using AMX tile instructions for high-throughput GEMM on the CPU side.
nv: A cooperative CPU-GPU inference framework that exploits AMX matrix extensions on modern Intel CPUs as a genuine compute peer to the GPU, combined with CXL memory integration for extended model capacity without multi-GPU cost.

mx.speedup: Up to 5.1x lower latency (Sapphire Rapids), up to 19x lower latency (Granite Rapids) vs latest single-GPU offloading; 3.7x-5.1x higher throughput
mx.other: CXL offloading yields additional 1.5x throughput; max batch size increased 1.8x (900-1.6K)

th: AMX CPU-GPU cooperative LLM inference with CXL memory offloading

t: Garibaldi: A Pairwise Instruction-Data Management for Enhancing Shared Last-Level Cache Performance in Server Workloads
pb: Server workloads suffer from a 'instruction victim' problem in the shared LLC: cold instruction cachelines are evicted by competing hot data cachelines, yet each instruction miss stalls the CPU frontend regardless of how much hot data is already resident in the LLC. Existing LLC management policies (Mockingjay, Hawkeye, DRRIP) optimize for data reuse distance and ignore the cost asymmetry between instruction and data misses.
me: Garibaldi introduces a pairwise instruction-data LLC management scheme built on three mechanisms: (1) a pair table (16K direct-mapped entries, 194 KB total) that tracks each instruction physical address alongside the hotness (miss_cost counter, 6-bit saturating) of the data cachelines it triggers; (2) a selective instruction protection policy using a query-based selection (QBS) mechanism that, at eviction time, queries the pair table and overrides the replacement policy to retain any instruction line whose aged miss_cost exceeds a dynamically adjusted threshold; (3) a pairwise prefetch that, upon serving an unprotected instruction miss, proactively issues prefetch requests for the associated cold data lines recorded in the pair table. Dynamic threshold adjustment uses a synchronized l-bit coloring timer that tracks P(D_miss | I_miss) every 100K LLC accesses and raises or lowers the protection threshold accordingly.
nv: Garibaldi is the first LLC management scheme to quantify the opportunity cost of instruction misses in terms of the hotness of the data they trigger, propagating data-line hotness back to instruction lines via a pair table and using it to drive selective eviction protection and prefetching.

mx.speedup: 13.2% geomean over LRU baseline (6.1% over Mockingjay alone) on 40-core server; up to 65.2% on verilator
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 10.4% energy reduction vs LRU (5.0% below Mockingjay alone)
mx.area: 193.9 KB total storage overhead for 40 cores (0.6% of 30 MB LLC)
mx.other: 18% reduction in ifetch stall cycles vs LRU with Mockingjay+Garibaldi

th: LLC pairwise instruction-data management for server frontend bottleneck

t: ANSMET: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Near-Memory Processing and Hybrid Early Termination
pb: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over large high-dimensional vector databases is both highly memory-bound and computationally wasteful: a large fraction of fetched vectors and their distance computations are ultimately discarded because many candidate vectors are far from the query. This dual inefficiency — excess memory traffic and low data utilization — limits throughput and energy efficiency on general-purpose computing platforms.
me: ANSMET co-designs a near-data processing (NDP) architecture at the memory rank level with a hybrid partial-dimension/bit early termination strategy. Distance calculation and comparison for ANNS are offloaded to near-data units within memory ranks, eliminating main memory bandwidth consumption for rejected vectors. As a vector is streamed from memory, ANSMET conservatively estimates a lower-bound distance using partial dimensions and/or partial bits of each element; if this lower bound already exceeds a threshold, the fetch and computation are terminated early. Data layout within a single memory access and across multiple memory ranks is co-optimized to match the early termination granularity, and a lightweight host-NDP coordination protocol manages index traversal and result sorting.
nv: The hybrid partial-dimension/bit early termination strategy conservatively estimates distance lower bounds during streaming to skip unnecessary data fetches, combined with rank-level near-data processing to eliminate host memory bandwidth consumption for rejected ANNS candidates.

mx.speedup: 5.26x average from NDP; additional 1.52x from hybrid early termination (total ~8x)

th: Near-memory processing with hybrid early termination for ANNS

t: Profile-Guided Temporal Prefetching
pb: Temporal prefetching for irregular memory access patterns (data-dependent structures, pointer-chasing) requires metadata to record and replay past access sequences; existing on-chip metadata storage schemes for temporal prefetchers have limited capacity, and prior software-guided approaches have failed to optimize metadata storage management effectively, leaving temporal prefetching 0.1% over baseline with profile-guided methods.
me: Prophet is a hardware-software co-designed framework that uses profile-guided methods to optimize on-chip metadata storage management for temporal prefetchers. Instead of tracing full access sequences, Prophet profiles programs using lightweight hardware counters, then injects hints (compiler annotations) into the program binary to guide the hardware temporal prefetcher's metadata storage management at runtime. Dynamic tuning of these hints allows the optimized binary to adapt to different program inputs without re-profiling. Prophet is designed to coexist with existing hardware temporal prefetchers: it provides optimized metadata management for frequently executed hot paths while the original hardware-only scheme handles less frequent paths.
nv: Prophet uses counter-based profiling (rather than trace-based) combined with binary-injected hints and dynamic runtime tuning to guide on-chip metadata storage management for temporal prefetchers, enabling adaptation to varying program inputs without re-profiling.

mx.speedup: 14.23% over Triangel (state-of-the-art temporal prefetcher); prior profile-guided methods achieved only 0.1%
mx.other: Negligible profiling, analysis, and instruction overhead

th: Profile-guided metadata management for hardware temporal prefetchers

t: HeterRAG: Heterogeneous Processing-in-Memory Acceleration for Retrieval-augmented Generation
pb: RAG systems face two distinct memory bottlenecks: the retrieval stage suffers from random/irregular memory access patterns causing low bandwidth utilization, while the generation stage is bandwidth-limited by frequent GEMV operations over large LLM weights. Additionally, maintaining large-scale knowledge bases creates a capacity bottleneck that HBM-based PIM alone cannot satisfy.
me: HeterRAG combines HBM-based PIM and DIMM-based PIM in a heterogeneous system: DIMM-based PIM provides low-cost, high-capacity storage for large knowledge bases and accelerates the irregular memory accesses of the retrieval stage, while HBM-based PIM handles bandwidth-intensive GEMV operations in the generation stage. The architecture maps each RAG stage to the PIM type best suited to its access characteristics, coordinating data movement between the two PIM domains.
nv: First heterogeneous PIM system that jointly addresses the capacity bottleneck of retrieval and the bandwidth bottleneck of LLM generation by pairing DIMM-based PIM with HBM-based PIM for RAG.

mx.other: quantitative results not stated in abstract

th: heterogeneous PIM for retrieval-augmented generation

t: OptiPIM: Optimizing Processing-in-Memory Acceleration Using Integer Linear Programming
pb: Efficient PIM acceleration requires precise software-hardware mapping that transforms application algorithms into PIM operations and data layouts, but existing PIM accelerators rely on manually tuned heuristics or exhaustive search, producing under-optimized mappings and/or prohibitively long optimization times.
me: OptiPIM formulates the PIM mapping problem as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem using a PIM-friendly mapping representation with accurate cost modeling that concisely covers the entire design space. The framework is implemented as a compiler pass inside the open-source MLIR framework, enabling it to consume PyTorch workloads and emit optimized mappings for PIM accelerators. OptiPIM generates optimal mappings within 4 minutes by exploiting the problem structure to make the ILP tractable.
nv: Formulation of PIM mapping as an ILP problem within MLIR, enabling provably optimal mapping generation for data-intensive applications on PIM accelerators in practical time.

mx.speedup: at least 1.9x over heuristic mappings
mx.other: optimization time: within 4 minutes

th: ILP-based optimal mapping for PIM accelerators

t: In-Storage Acceleration of Retrieval Augmented Generation as a Service
pb: As RAG deployments shift knowledge bases to persistent NVMe storage to handle ever-growing corpora, the Search & Retrieval phase — comprising embedding model inference, similarity/relevance search over dynamic data structures, and long-latency storage accesses — becomes the dominant bottleneck for end-to-end latency.
me: The paper proposes a metamorphic in-storage accelerator architecture embedded within NVMe storage devices. The in-storage accelerator is programmable to support diverse RAG retrieval algorithms, dynamic data structures (e.g., HNSW, IVF), and varying computational patterns. It executes smaller language models for query embedding generation entirely in-storage, while the final LLM generation runs on DGX A100 systems. The metamorphic design adapts its functional units to the retrieval algorithm at hand without requiring host CPU involvement in the hot path.
nv: A metamorphic (reconfigurable) in-storage accelerator that executes both embedding model inference and similarity search entirely within the storage device, eliminating retrieval-stage host CPU and DRAM round-trips.

mx.speedup: 4.3x over Xeon CPU + NVMe; 1.5x over A100 GPU + DRAM

th: in-storage accelerator for RAG retrieval and embedding

t: Light-weight Cache Replacement for Instruction Heavy Workloads
pb: Modern instruction-heavy workloads (e.g., server-side software with large code footprints) place heavy pressure on the last-level cache (LLC), and state-of-the-art LLC replacement policies designed for general workloads impose high hardware overhead yet provide little additional benefit over simple policies when aggressive prefetching is also present. Existing policies such as Mockingjay require complex prediction infrastructure that is not justified by their marginal gains for instruction-heavy access patterns.
me: PACIPV (Prefetch-Aware Coarse-grained Insertion and Promotion Vectors) generalizes the Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP) framework by parameterizing cache line insertion position and promotion position as configurable vectors rather than fixed rules. The design space of valid RRIP-based policies is enumerated exhaustively on a training workload set to find the optimal insertion and promotion vectors. The selected policy is prefetch-aware, distinguishing demand and prefetch accesses and assigning them different insertion/promotion behavior to prevent prefetch thrashing. The resulting hardware implementation uses simple counter logic with negligible area overhead compared to RRIP.
nv: Exhaustive search over the RRIP insertion/promotion vector design space to find prefetch-aware optimal coarse-grained LLC replacement policies, demonstrating that simple parameterized RRIP variants match or exceed complex learned replacement policies for instruction-heavy workloads.

mx.speedup: 3.3% over LRU baseline; +1.1% over SRRIP; within 0.1% of Mockingjay
mx.other: significantly less hardware overhead than Mockingjay

th: Lightweight LLC replacement for instruction-heavy workloads

t: DReX: Accurate and Scalable Dense Retrieval Acceleration via Algorithmic-Hardware Codesign
pb: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) used in RAG dense retrieval is dataset-specific and inherently low-recall, causing irrelevant or incomplete context to degrade LLM generation quality. Exact nearest-neighbor search is too compute- and bandwidth-intensive for conventional processors.
me: DReX combines two hardware tiers: in-DRAM logic performs early filtering by comparing query vectors against embedding centroids to eliminate distant candidates without moving full vectors off-chip, and an outside-DRAM near-memory accelerator then executes exact k-NN search on the filtered, much smaller candidate set. The in-DRAM filter exploits processing-in-memory (PIM) capabilities of commodity DRAM to compute approximate distance bounds, bypassing DRAM-to-processor transfers for the bulk of vectors. This two-stage pipeline minimizes off-chip data movement while guaranteeing exact retrieval on the survivors.
nv: Using in-DRAM logic for coarse vector filtering combined with a near-memory accelerator for exact search, eliminating the recall-versus-speed tradeoff of ANNS without bulk off-chip data movement.

mx.speedup: 6.2-7x reduction in time-to-first-token vs. state-of-the-art ANNS mechanism
mx.area: reasonable area and power overhead in memory subsystem (exact numbers not stated in abstract)

th: near-memory exact dense retrieval for RAG

t: ATiM: Autotuning Tensor Programs for Processing-in-DRAM
pb: Current software stacks for DRAM-PIM (specifically UPMEM) rely on hand-tuned libraries, lack high-level programming abstractions, and have no systematic optimization framework, making it difficult to achieve peak hardware utilization for tensor workloads including LLM layers.
me: ATiM is a search-based optimizing tensor compiler for the UPMEM DRAM-PIM architecture. It jointly searches the host-side and kernel-side tensor program space, applying PIM-aware optimizations to handle boundary conditions introduced by the banked DRAM layout. The compiler extends standard autotuning search algorithms to cover the expanded UPMEM-specific search space (e.g., tasklet counts, loop tiling, data placement across DPU banks), then generates fused, hardware-specific code without requiring manual library authoring.
nv: ATiM is the first tensor compiler to provide fully automated autotuning-integrated code generation for a DRAM-PIM system, bridging high-level tensor abstractions to UPMEM's banked-DRAM programming model.

mx.speedup: Up to 6.18x on UPMEM benchmark kernels; 8.21x on GPT-J layers

th: Autotuning tensor compiler for DRAM-PIM

t: Hybrid SLC-MLC RRAM Mixed-Signal Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Transformer Acceleration via Gradient Redistribution
pb: Analog RRAM PIM using multi-level cells (MLC) can offer 2x storage density and higher compute throughput than single-level cells (SLC), but MLC's non-linearity causes catastrophic accuracy degradation (e.g., 40% drop) in Transformer models, while brute-force hybrid SLC/MLC mapping fails to move enough weights into MLC to yield meaningful efficiency gains.
me: HyFlexPIM uses a three-tier mixed-signal RRAM PIM architecture: (1) digital SLC RRAM PIM for attention Q·K^T and ×V operations that require high precision and write real-time vectors, (2) analog SLC RRAM PIM for the most critical static weight rows, and (3) analog MLC RRAM PIM (2-bit per cell) for the error-tolerant majority of static weights. A single analog PIM module is reconfigurable between SLC and MLC via a shared 6-b/7-b flexible SAR-ADC that bypasses the MSB comparison in SLC mode, adding less than 1% area/energy overhead. On the software side, gradient redistribution applies SVD to decompose each linear weight matrix, truncates to a hard threshold rank to maintain iso-computational cost, then fine-tunes for 1-3 epochs with AdamW; the fine-tuning process naturally concentrates gradient magnitude into the top 5-10% of singular values, making those rows clearly demarcated as SLC-critical while 90-95% of weights are safely mapped to MLC.
nv: Gradient redistribution via SVD truncation followed by fine-tuning actively reshapes gradient distributions to concentrate critical weight importance into 5-10% of parameters, enabling 90-95% of Transformer weights to be computed in efficient MLC RRAM while preserving less than 1% accuracy loss.

mx.speedup: 1.86x max throughput over ASADI (SoA analog-digital hybrid PIM)
mx.area: 65nm technology node; <1% area overhead for SLC/MLC reconfigurability
mx.accuracy: <1% accuracy degradation for encoder (BERT) and vision (ViT); <10% loss increase for decoder (GPT-2, Llama3)
mx.other: 5-10% SLC protection rate sufficient for encoders; 5-20% for decoders

th: Hybrid SLC-MLC RRAM PIM with gradient redistribution for transformer inference

t: ArtMem: Adaptive Migration in Reinforcement Learning-Enabled Tiered Memory
pb: Tiered memory systems struggle with three key inefficiencies: existing migration policies perform inconsistently across workloads, fail to adapt when the fast-tier access rate is low, and miss opportunities to tune migration scope dynamically based on workload patterns, causing unnecessary page migrations.
me: ArtMem is a reinforcement learning (RL)-driven tiered memory management framework that dynamically adapts migration policy to evolving workload behavior. The RL agent observes fast-tier access rates and workload access patterns at runtime to decide page placement, migration scope (which pages to migrate and how many), and when to suppress migration entirely when the fast tier is underutilized. This closed-loop control replaces static thresholds with learned policies.
nv: Using a reinforcement learning agent to jointly control migration strategy selection, scope tuning, and suppression in response to live workload evolution in tiered memory.

mx.speedup: 35-172% performance improvement over state-of-the-art tiering systems

th: RL-driven adaptive tiered memory management

t: PuDHammer: Experimental Analysis of Read Disturbance Effects of Processing-using-DRAM in Real DRAM Chips
pb: Processing-using-DRAM (PuD) operations require multiple-row activation (activating multiple DRAM rows simultaneously or in quick succession), a fundamentally different access pattern from conventional single-row activation. No prior work has characterized whether this multiple-row activation exacerbates DRAM read disturbance (RowHammer-style bitflips) compared to standard single-row activation.
me: The authors conduct an experimental characterization study (PuDHammer) using 316 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major manufacturers. They test multiple-row activation patterns (as used by PuD bulk bitwise operations) across a sweep of operational parameters: temperature, data patterns, access patterns (simultaneous vs. sequential row activation), DRAM timing parameters, and spatial variation within chips. They measure the minimum hammer count (HC_first) required to induce the first bitflip and compare to conventional single-row RowHammer.
nv: First experimental characterization of how PuD-style multiple-row activation affects DRAM read disturbance on real DDR4 chips, showing PuDHammer can reduce the bitflip threshold by up to 158.58x compared to standard RowHammer.

mx.other: HC_first (minimum hammer count to first bitflip) reduced by up to 158.58x vs. RowHammer on 316 real DDR4 chips

th: DRAM read disturbance characterization for PuD operations

t: UGPU: Dynamically Constructing Unbalanced GPUs for Enhanced Resource Efficiency
pb: Physical GPUs maintain a fixed, balanced ratio of compute and memory resources, which is inefficient when co-executing workloads have heterogeneous compute-to-memory demands. Partitioning a GPU into unbalanced slices requires accurate performance prediction under variable resource allocations and causes heavy data migration overhead when memory resources are redistributed.
me: UGPU dynamically carves a single physical GPU into unbalanced GPU slices—each with a tailored compute-SM count and HBM capacity—using a demand-aware resource partitioning algorithm that avoids complex analytical performance models. To handle memory redistribution without incurring the latency of traditional page migration, it introduces PageMove, which exploits the fact that all HBM memory channels share physical TSV connections within the DRAM stack, enabling parallel page migration between bank groups. PageMove pairs a customized memory address mapping with a Parallel Page Migration Mode (PPMM) and updated virtual memory management to move pages across memory dies at high throughput concurrently.
nv: PageMove exploits pre-existing intra-stack TSV connectivity and simultaneous multi-bank-group transfers in HBM to execute parallel page migration between memory dies, eliminating the dominant overhead of dynamic GPU slice reconfiguration.

mx.speedup: not explicitly quantified in abstract
mx.other: PageMove reduces page migration overhead vs. traditional migration (magnitude not stated in abstract)

th: dynamic unbalanced GPU resource partitioning for multi-tenant efficiency

t: Stratum: System-Hardware Co-Design with Tiered Monolithic 3D-Stackable DRAM for Efficient MoE Serving
pb: MoE LLM inference is bottlenecked by the massive expert parameter volume (>95% of model size in models like Mixtral 8x7B), which overwhelms GPU HBM bandwidth and capacity; HBM-based NMP approaches are further limited by coarse-pitch TSV interconnects (~10 µm) that cap internal bandwidth.
me: Stratum integrates Mono3D DRAM with NMP logic via Cu-Cu hybrid bonding on a logic die, connected to GPU via 2.5D silicon interposer. Within the Mono3D DRAM stack, an in-memory tiering mechanism assigns expert weights to fast (low wordline-staircase latency) or slow tiers based on predicted access frequency. A lightweight topic classifier predicts which experts will be hot for a given batch of user queries and re-maps them to fast tiers before each batch via a row-swap buffer. The NMP processor on the logic die includes per-channel Processing Units (PUs) connected via a ring network, each containing near-bank PE clusters with tensor cores executing GeMM/GeMV, an intra-channel reducer, and a SIMD special-function engine for Softmax/SiLU. The prefill phase runs on the GPU (xPU) and decoding runs on Stratum NMP.
nv: In-memory tiering exploits inherent access-latency heterogeneity across Mono3D DRAM wordline layers, combined with topic-based expert usage prediction, to maximally concentrate hot expert weights in fast DRAM tiers without off-chip data movement.

mx.speedup: up to 8.29x decoding throughput improvement vs. GPU baseline
mx.energy_or_tops_w: up to 7.66x better energy efficiency vs. GPU baseline
mx.other: Mono3D DRAM internal bandwidth: ~5x higher vertical interconnect density than HBM (1 µm vs 10 µm TSV pitch)

th: Mono3D DRAM NMP system for MoE LLM inference with in-memory tiering

t: Chasoñ: Supporting Cross HBM Channel Data Migration to Enable Efficient Sparse Algebraic Acceleration
pb: HBM-based sparse accelerators suffer from high resource underutilization due to static non-zero scheduling that cannot redistribute work across HBM channels when data access patterns are irregular. Existing designs like Serpens fix data-to-channel mapping, leaving processing elements idle when a channel has no work.
me: Chaso is an FPGA-based streaming HBM accelerator for SpMV that introduces Cross-HBM Channel out-of-Order Scheduling (CrHCS), which dynamically migrates non-zero data across HBM channels at runtime to balance load. When one channel's processing elements are starved, CrHCS identifies data in other channels and migrates it, enabling out-of-order execution across channel boundaries. The design is implemented on AMD Alveo U55C running at 301 MHz, targeting the SuiteSparse and SNAP matrix collections.
nv: CrHCS is the first non-zero scheduling scheme that permits out-of-order cross-channel data migration in HBM-based sparse accelerators, directly addressing per-channel load imbalance.

mx.speedup: up to 8x over Serpens, 20.33x over RTX 4090, 11.65x over RTX 6000 Ada, 2.67x over Core i9-11980HK
mx.other: 301 MHz on AMD Alveo U55C

th: HBM-aware dynamic scheduling for sparse linear algebra acceleration

t: Micro-MAMA: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Multicore Prefetching
pb: Independent RL-based prefetchers on each core of a multicore system compete for shared memory bandwidth without coordination, causing each agent to greedily claim excessive bandwidth and converging to sub-optimal system-wide policies. This problem is an instance of the multi-agent credit assignment and non-stationarity challenge in MARL.
me: MAMA uses a two-tier architecture: distributed local multi-armed bandit agents on each core narrow the joint-action search space by selecting among local prefetch aggressiveness options, while a central supervisor agent with global bandwidth visibility learns joint policies that maximize system-wide throughput or fairness. Key local agents receive system-level perspective signals (estimated global bandwidth usage) to discourage actions that harm other cores. The supervisor uses a lightweight bandit over the local agents' reduced action space, avoiding the exponential joint-action blow-up of fully centralized control.
nv: A hierarchical supervisor that provides global bandwidth perspective to local bandit prefetchers, enabling coordinated joint policies without requiring centralized control of all per-core decisions.

mx.speedup: 2.1% throughput improvement over independent agents; 10.4% fairness improvement
mx.other: 8-core simulated system evaluation

th: Multi-agent RL for coordinated multicore prefetch policy learning

t: A TRRIP Down Memory Lane: Temperature-Based Re-Reference Interval Prediction For Instruction Caching
pb: Modern mobile CPU workloads (interpreters, JIT compilers, UI frameworks) have large instruction footprints with long reuse distances that defeat hardware-only cache replacement policies, causing persistent L2 instruction cache miss stalls even after PGO code layout optimization.
me: TRRIP is a compiler-OS-hardware co-design cache replacement policy. The LLVM PGO compiler classifies basic blocks as hot/warm/cold by execution frequency and places them in separate ELF sections (.text.hot, .text.warm, .text.cold). The OS loader reads these ELF headers and encodes temperature (2 bits) into existing ARM PBHA bits in page table entries (PTEs), requiring no ISA changes. The MMU transfers temperature bits with every memory request to the L2 cache. The hardware replacement policy extends RRIP: hot instruction lines are inserted at Immediate re-reference priority (RRPV=0), warm lines at Near (RRPV=1), cold/data lines at Intermediate (RRPV=2) per the existing RRIP eviction scan. The variant TRRIP-2 additionally decelerates RRPV promotion for non-hot hits. No additional on-chip storage is required beyond existing PTE bits.
nv: Using existing ARM PBHA page-table bits as a zero-storage-overhead channel to pass compiler-derived hot/cold temperature to the L2 cache replacement policy without ISA modifications.

mx.speedup: 3.9% geomean over SRRIP baseline (PGO-compiled mobile benchmarks)
mx.other: L2 instruction MPKI reduction of 26.5% (TRRIP-1) and 27.3% (TRRIP-2)

th: Temperature-aware instruction cache replacement via compiler-OS-hardware co-design

t: Pimba: A Processing-in-Memory Acceleration for Post-Transformer Large Language Model Serving
pb: Post-transformer LLMs (SSMs such as Mamba-2, linear attention, RNNs) and transformer-based LLMs both become memory-bandwidth-bound during batched inference due to state update and attention operations respectively, but the diverse primitives in state updates (element-wise multiply, outer product, GEMV) make per-bank PIM acceleration area-prohibitive, and existing LLM quantization formats degrade accuracy severely on SU-LLMs due to the swamping effect.
me: Pimba implements a PIM accelerator array where each State-update Processing Unit (SPU) is shared between two DRAM banks via access interleaving: while one bank is being read, the paired bank writes its result, enabling continuous utilization of a single pipelined SPU without throughput loss. Each SPU contains a State-update Processing Engine (SPE) with custom MX8 multipliers and adders (MX format with 8-bit shared exponent and 1-bit microexponents, 16 elements per group, using stochastic rounding). The four-stage SPE pipeline executes: (1) state fetch, (2) state decay plus outer product in parallel, (3) accumulate, (4) GEMV output and write-back. KV-cache attention is accelerated by reusing the same SPU logic in an attention mode dataflow. The system offloads state update and attention to PIM during the generation phase while the GPU handles prefill and other operations.
nv: Sharing one pipelined SPU between two DRAM banks via access interleaving halves PIM area overhead compared to per-bank designs while maintaining the same throughput.

mx.speedup: up to 4.1x token generation throughput over LLM-optimized GPU; up to 2.1x over GPU+PIM baseline; 14.6x lower state-update latency vs GPU
mx.other: Area overhead described as minimal on DRAM device; MX8 achieves near fp16 perplexity on Mamba-2/RetNet/GLA/HGRN2

th: PIM accelerator for post-transformer LLM serving with interleaved bank sharing

t: CrossBit: Bitwise Computing in NAND Flash Memory with Inter-Bitline Data Communication
pb: Existing in-flash processing (IFP) architectures can only perform bitwise operations on data sensed within the same bitline, preventing computation involving data from different bitlines. This restriction makes prior IFP designs unable to implement error correction codes (ECC) or efficiently process database query operations that require inter-bitline data interactions.
me: CrossBit extends commodity NAND flash memory with minimal additional circuitry to support both intra-bitline and inter-bitline bulk bitwise operations. It introduces inter-bitline communication pathways that allow data sensed from different bitlines to interact during in-flash compute. This enables in-flash ECC (IF-ECC) operations directly on MLC flash cells, which eliminates the prior restriction to SLC-only IFP. The same inter-bitline capability is leveraged to accelerate fundamental database selection and join queries that previously required data movement across bitlines.
nv: CrossBit is the first IFP architecture to support inter-bitline data communication during in-flash computation, enabling reliable MLC-based IFP through in-flash ECC and substantially expanding the class of operations executable within NAND flash memory.

mx.speedup: 2.1x over SOTA IFP for database queries; 1.7x on Star Schema Benchmark end-to-end
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 2.5x energy efficiency improvement over SOTA IFP
mx.other: 1.8x bit density increase using MLC vs SLC in prior IFP

th: inter-bitline in-flash computation for databases and MLC ECC

t: ORCHES: Orchestrated Test-Time-Compute-based LLM Reasoning on Collaborative GPU-PIM HEterogeneous System
pb: Test-time compute (TTC) inference pipelines for LLM reasoning on edge devices suffer from three bottlenecks: variable parallelism due to inference-dependent dynamic control flow and varying batch sizes; branch dependencies that stall sequential reasoning steps; and branch pruning causing memory fragmentation and irregular access patterns.
me: ORCHES is a GPU-PIM collaborative system that partitions LLM reasoning workloads between a GPU and Processing-in-Memory (PIM) units. Three key mechanisms address the identified bottlenecks: (1) adaptive workload assignment dynamically balances computation between GPU and PIM based on real-time branching patterns; (2) branch-aware pipelining uses speculative execution to overlap reasoning steps and reduce inter-step pipeline stalls from branch dependencies; (3) fragmentation-aware memory structuring improves data locality through coordinated caching strategies and optimized memory layout reorganization to handle irregular access caused by branch pruning.
nv: Branch-aware pipelining with speculative execution specifically designed for TTC reasoning control flow, combined with adaptive GPU-PIM workload splitting that responds to dynamic branching at inference time.

mx.speedup: 4.16x over SOTA GPU (text-based TTC reasoning); 3.10x over SOTA GPU (vision-based TTC reasoning)

th: GPU-PIM collaborative system for test-time-compute LLM reasoning

t: Symbiotic Task Scheduling and Data Prefetching
pb: Hardware task-parallel systems that operate with fine-grained tasks (approx. 100-cycle execution time) cannot benefit from conventional hardware prefetchers because tasks are too short for prefetches to complete before the task finishes, leaving DRAM latency fully exposed and undermining the performance gains of hardware task management.
me: The Task-Seeded Prefetcher (TSP) learns the data-access pattern of each task function type and issues prefetches as soon as a task descriptor is queued by the hardware task scheduler, using the descriptor as a seed to identify which memory addresses the task will access. The Memory Response Task Scheduler (MRS) augments the baseline task-to-core dispatch policy by monitoring prefetch completion status from TSP: when a task's prefetches are done, MRS preferentially dispatches it to a ready core, maximizing prefetch utilization without stalling the pipeline. Together, TSP and MRS form a symbiotic pair where scheduling drives prefetching and prefetch status informs scheduling.
nv: A symbiotic co-design of a function-aware task-seeded prefetcher (TSP) and a prefetch-status-aware task scheduler (MRS) that together exploit the task descriptor queue as an early prefetch trigger in hardware task-parallel systems.

mx.speedup: up to 3.1x; geometric mean up to 1.4x across 13 benchmarks on 256-core systems

th: symbiotic task-seeded prefetching and scheduling for hardware task-parallel systems

t: FALA: Locality-Aware PIM-Host Cooperation for Graph Processing with Fine-Grained Column Access
pb: Graph processing exhibits irregular memory access patterns that cause significant memory bandwidth waste on DRAM architectures: cache-based graph tiling suffers from overfetching due to the mismatch between DRAM burst size and the sparse data actually needed, while PIM-based approaches fail to exploit cache locality for high-reuse workloads.
me: FALA is a hybrid architecture integrating PIM and cache-based acceleration. It introduces a fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM memory banks that allows selective access to individual columns (vertices) rather than fetching full DRAM rows, eliminating overfetching for sparse graph accesses. A locality-aware PIM architecture is designed to route accesses: high-reuse vertex data is served through the host CPU cache hierarchy, while low-reuse, irregular accesses are processed near-memory via PIM. The design minimizes unnecessary memory traffic while fully utilizing both internal DRAM bandwidth and on-chip caches.
nv: A fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM banks that enables PIM to process individual graph vertices without loading full DRAM rows, combined with a locality-aware policy that routes reused data through host caches and irregular accesses through PIM.

mx.speedup: 1.56x geometric mean speedup vs. prior art

th: locality-aware PIM-host cooperation for graph processing with fine-grained DRAM column access

t: Drishti: Do Not Forget Slicing While Designing Last-Level Cache Replacement Policies for Many-Core Systems
pb: State-of-the-art LLC replacement policies (Hawkeye, Mockingjay) use a per-slice sampled cache and a per-slice reuse predictor that make myopic decisions based only on accesses to a single slice, unaware of global reuse behavior across all LLC slices in many-core systems; additionally, per-slice sampled cache sets receive insufficient LLC misses to drive accurate replacement decisions.
me: Drishti proposes two enhancements to existing LLC replacement policies for sliced LLCs: (1) a per-core global reuse predictor where each core's predictor is trained on all accesses by that core across all LLC slices—achieving global reuse awareness without centralized inter-slice interconnect traffic—combined with a local (per-slice) sampled cache that remains slice-local; (2) a per-slice dynamic sampled cache that adaptively expands the set of LLC sets used for sampling to improve the sample quality and ensure adequate miss coverage per slice. Evaluated by augmenting Hawkeye and Mockingjay on 4, 16, and 32-core systems with 8, 32, and 64 MB sliced LLCs.
nv: Decoupling the reuse predictor (per-core, globally aware) from the sampled cache (per-slice, local) in sliced LLC replacement policies, enabling global reuse inference without centralized interconnect traffic.

mx.speedup: 5.6% IPC improvement (Hawkeye+Drishti) and 13.2% (Mockingjay+Drishti) over LRU on 32-core system
mx.other: Without Drishti: Hawkeye 3.3%, Mockingjay 6.7% over LRU; Drishti roughly doubles the gain

th: sliced-LLC-aware last-level cache replacement policy design

t: LLM.265: Video Codecs are Secretly Tensor Codecs
pb: LLM training and inference are increasingly bottlenecked by memory footprint and communication bandwidth for weights, activations, gradients, and KV cache, but existing tensor-compression methods are specialized for only one type of tensor and require custom hardware or software stacks. A unified, bandwidth-efficient compression mechanism applicable across all LLM tensor types is missing.
me: LLM.265 repurposes existing GPU hardware video encoders/decoders (H.265/HEVC engines) as general-purpose tensor codecs. The key insight is that LLM tensors expose spatial and temporal statistical structure (smooth weight manifolds, slowly changing activations, correlated KV cache vectors) that codec stages — inter-frame prediction, DCT/transform coding, scalar quantization, and entropy coding via context-adaptive arithmetic coding — can exploit directly. The system maps tensor layouts to frame formats, applies intra/inter prediction to exploit tensor correlations, and uses entropy coding to compress residuals. Custom hardware extensions to the existing video engine improve tensor encoding/decoding throughput without major GPU architecture changes.
nv: Reusing commodity GPU video codec hardware engines as unified tensor compressors for all LLM data types (weights, activations, gradients, KV cache), eliminating the need for specialized compression accelerators.

mx.other: Compression effectiveness for weights, activations, gradients, KV cache not stated in abstract; throughput vs. baseline not stated

th: GPU video codec hardware repurposed as LLM tensor compressor

t: ColumnDisturb: Understanding Column-based Read Disturbance in Real DRAM Chips and Implications for Future Systems
pb: A newly discovered DRAM read disturbance phenomenon called ColumnDisturb allows a single aggressor row activation to disturb DRAM cells through bitlines (columns), inducing bitflips in rows sharing the same columns across multiple subarrays — up to 3072 rows simultaneously in DDR4 — which is fundamentally different from RowHammer/RowPress that affect only a few adjacent rows in a single subarray.
me: The paper conducts a rigorous experimental characterization of ColumnDisturb on 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major DRAM manufacturers. Experiments vary temperature, data patterns, DRAM timing parameters (tRCD, tRAS, tRP), average bitline voltage, memory access patterns, and spatial variation across chips. The study measures minimum time to first bitflip, affected row count, and bitflip counts under nominal 63.6ms DDR4 refresh windows. The authors compare ColumnDisturb severity against DRAM retention failures and perform cycle-level simulation to quantify the impact on retention-aware refresh mechanisms that propose to skip refreshes for cells with long retention times.
nv: First experimental demonstration and comprehensive characterization of ColumnDisturb — a column/bitline-mediated read disturbance affecting up to 3 subarrays simultaneously from a single aggressor row, fundamentally broader in spatial scope than RowHammer.

mx.other: First-bitflip time reduces by up to 5.06x (2.96x average) with smaller DRAM node; affects up to 3072 rows simultaneously; induces bitflips within 63.6ms DDR4 refresh window on real chips; up to 198x more affected rows than retention failures

th: New DRAM column-based read disturbance phenomenon characterization

t: Characterizing and Optimizing Realistic Workloads on a Commercial Compute-in-SRAM Device
pb: Prior compute-in-SRAM evaluations rely on simulators or small prototypes, so the real-world performance and energy efficiency of commercial devices under realistic AI workloads (particularly retrieval-augmented generation over large corpora) is not well understood, and programming principles for exploiting the architecture's 2-million bit-processor parallelism are largely unknown.
me: The paper characterizes the commercial GSI APU (2M 1-bit processors at 500 MHz, 25 TOPS, 26 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, 12MB L1 / 64KB L2 / 1MB L3 / 16GB DDR) using the Phoenix benchmark suite and matrix multiplication microbenchmarks, and develops a Python-based analytical framework modeling non-uniform data movement costs across 4 memory levels (L1-L4) and intra-VR vs. inter-VR operations. Three optimizations are proposed and validated on real hardware: (1) communication-aware reduction mapping that maps the reduction axis temporally to cheaper inter-VR operations (scalar-vector product) rather than costly intra-VR spatial reduction; (2) DMA coalescing via subgroup copy to eliminate redundant off-chip data duplication across loop iterations; and (3) broadcast-friendly data layouts that reduce L3 lookup table sizes from K*N to N elements to cut broadcast latency. These optimizations are applied to RAG retrieval over 10-200GB corpora.
nv: First comprehensive real-hardware evaluation of a commercial compute-in-SRAM device (GSI APU) under realistic AI workloads, revealing that even compute-in-SRAM can be bandwidth-bound without careful data layout optimization, and demonstrating three concrete optimizations that approach the compute roofline.

mx.speedup: 4.8x-6.6x retrieval speedup over optimized CPU; 1.1x-1.8x end-to-end RAG latency improvement; matches NVIDIA A6000 GPU latency for RAG
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 54.4x-117.9x energy reduction vs. NVIDIA A6000 GPU for RAG; 41.8x speedup over CPU on Phoenix benchmarks

th: Real-hardware compute-in-SRAM characterization and optimization for RAG

t: NEO: Saving GPU Memory Crisis with CPU Offloading for Online LLM Inference
pb: GPU memory limits LLM inference batch size, wasting GPU compute; existing CPU offloading systems either hurt latency (symmetric pipelining bubbles) or require expensive dedicated CPUs.
me: NEO asymmetric GPU-CPU pipelining: each iteration splits into two sub-batches. Batch-0 (all prefill requests + most decode requests) runs a long linear projection stage on GPU. Batch-1 (CPU-assigned decode requests) runs a long attention stage on CPU — both overlap. KV cache split into GPU-cache (HBM) and CPU-cache (DRAM). Layer-wise KV swap overlaps PCIe transfer with GPU compute. Load-aware scheduler uses offline-profiled time models + linear interpolation to greedily assign requests per iteration, comparing GPU-only vs asymmetric pipelining and choosing higher throughput. ISPC-compiled SPMD CPU attention kernels (PACPU) with paged attention, SIMD loads, and Flash Decoding-style parallelism across cores.
nv: Asymmetric sub-batch design that integrates prefill into the GPU batch to extend GPU-stage duration, hiding CPU attention latency and eliminating symmetric pipelining bubbles.

mx.speedup: Up to 7.5x throughput on T4, 26% on A10G, 14% on H100 vs GPU-only; up to 79.3% with higher-bandwidth CPUs

t: GSplit: Scaling Graph Neural Network Training on Large Graphs via Probabilistic Splitting
pb: Mini-batch GNN training with data parallelism causes significant redundant feature loading and computation because the same graph vertices appear in multiple GPU micro-batches, limiting scalability to large graphs.
me: Split parallelism: each mini-batch is sampled once and non-overlappingly partitioned (split) on-the-fly among GPUs using an offline probabilistic splitting algorithm. The offline phase uses pre-sampling to weight graph vertices and edges by expected sampling frequency, then applies weighted min-edge-cut partitioning (METIS) to find a global vertex-to-GPU assignment. Online splitting maps each sampled vertex to its pre-assigned GPU in constant time. Inter-GPU feature shuffles at each GNN layer exchange only required features.
nv: Online probabilistic splitting that reduces NP-hard per-mini-batch partitioning to a constant-time lookup by leveraging an offline pre-sampled weighted graph partition, providing provable expected communication minimization and load balancing.

mx.speedup: Up to 4.4x over DGL (2.5x average), 4.1x over P3 (2.4x average), 1.9x over Quiver (1.4x average) on Orkut/Papers100M/Friendster graphs
mx.accuracy: No accuracy loss vs data-parallel training (verified on Papers100M)

t: A Bring-Your-Own-Model Approach for ML-Driven Storage Placement in Warehouse-Scale Computers
pb: ML-based storage tiering (SSD vs HDD placement) cannot be practically deployed at Google-scale because a monolithic model in the storage layer must be retrained whenever any workload changes, breaks separation of concerns, and becomes a single point of failure across heterogeneous workloads.
me: Bring-Your-Own-Model (BYOM): each workload trains its own lightweight gradient-boosted trees model at the application layer, not in the storage layer. The model predicts an 'importance' ranking category for each shuffle job based on application-level features (execution metadata, allocated resources, historical I/O metrics, timestamps). Importance categories are designed by analyzing oracle placement decisions under varying SSD capacities: category 0 = negative TCO savings, categories 1-N = I/O density quantiles. At the storage layer, an Adaptive Category Selection (ACS) algorithm uses a sliding admission threshold driven by real-time SSD spillover TCIO feedback, dynamically adjusting which importance categories are admitted to SSD without needing to retrain the model.
nv: Cross-layer ML+heuristic design where application-layer per-workload gradient-boosted trees predict environment-agnostic importance rankings, and a storage-layer adaptive algorithm translates rankings to placement decisions using real-time capacity feedback—separating ML concerns from system concerns.

t: Training Ultra Long Context Language Model with Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer
pb: Training LLMs on extremely long sequences (1M+ tokens) requires memory far exceeding GPU capacity; existing Ulysses-style sequence parallelism is bottlenecked by PCIe transfer latency when offloading to host memory.
me: Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer (FPDT) extends DeepSpeed Ulysses with CPU memory offloading using a double-buffer design. The sequence is sliced into chunks (default 64K tokens). A pipeline overlaps PCIe host-to-device prefetch of the next chunk with GPU computation on the current chunk. A rank-ordinal scatter redistributes activations across GPUs. The vocabulary computation is also pipelined within the sequence chunk pipeline.
nv: Double-buffer design that hides PCIe latency behind computation, enabling 16x longer sequences than state-of-the-art on the same hardware while maintaining >55% MFU. First system to train 8B LLM with 2M sequence length on only 4 GPUs.

mx.sequence_length_improvement: 16x over prior SOTA on same hardware

t: Graph Learning at Scale: Characterizing and Optimizing Pre-Propagation GNNs
pb: Pre-propagation GNNs (PP-GNNs), which decouple feature propagation from training as a preprocessing step, suffer from data loading as their dominant bottleneck (88-91% of training time) and face severe scalability challenges from input expansion (K(R+1)x larger inputs).
me: The paper characterizes PP-GNN bottlenecks and proposes: (1) Chunk reshuffling that performs coarser shuffling enabling GPU-side batch assembly to replace fine-grained row-level shuffling; (2) Double-buffer prefetching to overlap I/O with computation; (3) GPU Direct Storage (GDS) for graphs exceeding host memory; (4) Tailored training strategies (mini-batch GD and chunk-based sampling) to handle input expansion. These optimizations target the I/O path from SSD/storage to GPU.
nv: First systematic characterization of PP-GNN training revealing data loading (not compute) as the bottleneck, plus chunk reshuffling that enables efficient GPU-side batch assembly without fine-grained per-row I/O.
wl: Node classification on large graphs (ogbn-papers100M, MAG240M)

mx.vs_sampling_gnn: Up to 100x speedup on large graph benchmarks

t: Youmu: Efficient Columnar Data Pipeline for LLM Training
pb: LLM training datasets stored in columnar formats (Parquet) must be converted to other formats before training, wasting terabytes of storage. Direct use of columnar data causes 100x+ efficiency drops due to granularity mismatch between coarse columnar chunk I/O (100s of MB) and fine-grained random access needed for shuffling.
me: YOUMU uses page-level data granularity as its core mechanism. The control plane builds a global page index spanning all Parquet files by collecting metadata at initialization; an index translator uses layered binary search to map random page IDs to physical locations. The data plane reads compressed pages directly from SSDs and decodes them using metadata. An aggressive buffer shuffle reads new pages into a fixed-size buffer as data is consumed, providing continuous in-buffer shuffling. Implemented in ~500 lines of Rust with PyO3 Python bindings.
nv: Page-level (KB-to-MB granularity) direct access to Parquet columnar data for LLM training, eliminating format conversion while achieving near-perfect shuffle quality via global page shuffling across multi-billion pages of TB-scale datasets.
